Apply at first rust appearance. Repeat after 10-14 days if needed. Use resistant varieties (LS-1 LS-2).

question: What fungicides are recommended for controlling powdery mildew in linseed?
answer: 1) Sulfur (80% WP) 500g/acre - effective cheap. 2) Tebuconazole 250ml/acre. 3) Propiconazole 250ml/acre. 4) Myclobutanil 200g/acre. 5) Hexaconazole 250ml/acre. 6) Dinocap (Karathane) 400ml/acre. Apply at first sign of white powder. Sulfur is organic-friendly. Avoid sulfur when temperature >30°C (phytotoxicity).

question: What fungicides are recommended for controlling blight in linseed in Pakistan?
answer: 1) Mancozeb (Dithane M-45) 500g/acre - protectant. 2) Chlorothalonil (Bravo) 500ml/acre. 3) Copper oxychloride 400g/acre. 4) Propiconazole 250ml/acre. 5) Azoxystrobin (Amistar) 200ml/acre. Apply at bud to early flowering stage. Repeat every 10-14 days if wet conditions persist. Use certified disease-free seed.

question: What fungicides are recommended for controlling wilt in linseed in Pakistan?
answer: Wilt (Fusarium) is difficult to control with fungicides once symptoms appear. Prevention: 1) Seed treatment with Carbendazim 2g/kg + Thiram 2g/kg. 2) Soil drench with Carbendazim 500g/acre (early stages). 3) Trichoderma harzianum (bio-fungicide) 2kg/acre in furrow at sowing. 4) Use resistant varieties (LS-1 LS-2). 5) Crop rotation (4-5 years with cereals).

question: What bactericides are used for bacterial diseases of linseed in Pakistan?
answer: Bacterial diseases are rare in linseed. If bacterial blight occurs: 1) Copper oxychloride 400g/acre. 2) Streptomycin + Tetracycline (Agrimycin) 100g/acre. 3) Kasugamycin 200ml/acre. Not routinely needed. Prevention: clean seed good sanitation.

question: What is the spray schedule for disease management in linseed in Pakistan?
answer: Rust-prone areas (Pothwar): 1st spray at bud stage (Dec-Jan) if rust seen. 2nd spray 10-14 days later. Powdery mildew: Spray when first white powder seen (Jan-Feb). Alternaria: Pre-flowering spray (Jan) if history. General schedule: Monitor weekly from December. Spray only when disease reaches threshold (e.g. rust pustules on 5-10% leaves). Use protectant fungicides (Mancozeb) before disease arrives.

question: What is the correct dose and method of fungicide application on linseed?
answer: 1) Calculate field area and required product dose. 2) Use 100-120 liters water per acre. 3) Add fungicide to water while agitating. 4) Use flat fan or hollow cone nozzles. 5) Spray to cover all leaves (upper and lower). 6) For rust/mildew: ensure good coverage. 7) Spray in morning (6-9 AM). 8) Avoid spraying during flowering if possible (protect bees).

question: What systemic vs. contact fungicides are recommended for linseed?
answer: Systemic (absorbed by plant): Tebuconazole Propiconazole Azoxystrobin - curative (can be used after infection) longer protection (10-14 days). Contact (surface only): Mancozeb Chlorothalonil Copper oxychloride Sulfur - preventive (must be applied before infection) shorter protection (5-7 days). Strategy: Use protectants early then systemics when disease appears. Alternate both to prevent resistance.

question: How often should fungicide be sprayed during the linseed growing season?
answer: Depends on disease pressure: Low pressure: 0-1 spray (only if disease appears). Moderate pressure: 2 sprays at 10-14 day interval. High pressure (Pothwar rust): 2-3 sprays (Dec-Jan-Feb). Do not exceed 3 sprays to avoid resistance and cost. Stop spraying after capsule filling stage (100 days).

question: What are the bio-fungicides or organic disease control methods for linseed?
answer: 1) Trichoderma harzianum (2kg/acre) soil application for wilt control. 2) Pseudomonas fluorescens (bio-control agent) seed treatment. 3) Sulfur (organic approved) for powdery mildew. 4) Neem oil (0.5%) for mildew and rust suppression. 5) Cow urine (10% solution) as foliar spray (traditional). 6) Baking soda (1%) + vegetable oil (0.5%) for mildew. 7) Crop rotation (3-4 years). 8) Resistant varieties (LS-1 LS-2).

question: When is linseed ready for harvest in Pakistan?
answer: Linseed is ready for harvest in March to April (110-140 days after sowing). Punjab: late March to mid-April. Sindh: early to late March. KPK: mid-April to early May. Balochistan: April to May. Harvest when 75-80% of capsules turn brown and seeds rattle inside.

question: What are the visual signs that linseed has reached maturity and is ready to harvest?
answer: 1) Capsules: 75-80% golden brown to brown. 2) Seeds: Rattle inside when shaken. 3) Stems: Turn yellow-brown. 4) Leaves: Most have dropped. 5) Seeds: Hard shiny with characteristic color (brown/yellow). 6) Moisture content: 20-25% in seeds. Do not delay - over-ripe capsules shatter causing seed loss.

question: What is the recommended moisture content of linseed at time of harvest?
answer: Harvest at 20-25% seed moisture content. At this stage: 1) Seeds are mature but not too dry. 2) Minimal shattering during harvest. 3) Can be manually cut without excessive loss. After harvest dry to 8-10% moisture for storage. Use moisture meter or traditional method (bite test - hard).

question: How is linseed harvested in Pakistan — manually (Daranti) or mechanically?
answer: Manual harvesting (dominant): 1) Using daranti (sickle) to cut plants close to ground. 2) Plants tied in small bundles (sheaves). 3) Stacked in field for 5-7 days drying. Mechanical: Combine harvester (increasing adoption) - cuts threshes and cleans in one operation. Also use reaper (cuts only) + thresher. Mechanical reduces labor cost but may cause more shattering if not adjusted.

question: What machinery (Combine Harvester/Thresher) is used for harvesting linseed in Pakistan?
answer: 1) Combine harvester (e.g. New Holland John Deere) - for large fields (>5 acres). Settings: Cylinder speed 400-500 RPM concave clearance wide to avoid seed cracking. 2) Reaper (tractor-mounted) - cuts plants windrows then pick up with thresher. 3) Stationary thresher - for manually harvested bundles. 4) Manual beating - on tarpaulin (traditional). Hire combine service: Rs. 2

question: How should linseed be harvested to minimize shattering or field losses?
answer: 1) Harvest at 75-80% capsule brownness (not fully dry). 2) Harvest early morning when dew present (capsules less brittle). 3) Use sharp sickles (clean cut reduces shatter). 4) Handle bundles gently - don't shake. 5) For combine: reduce cylinder speed (400-500 RPM). 6) Keep header low (3-5 cm above ground). 7) Harvest promptly - don't leave over-ripe in field. 8) Losses can be 10-20% if mismanaged.

question: What is the correct harvesting time for linseed in Punjab?
answer: Punjab: March 20 to April 20. North/Central Punjab (Rawalpindi Faisalabad): April 1-20. South Punjab (Multan Bahawalpur): March 20-April 10. Harvest when capsules brown. In Pothwar rainfed: late April due to later sowing.

question: What is the correct harvesting time for linseed in Sindh?
answer: Sindh: March 1 to March 30. Upper Sindh (Jacobabad Shikarpur): March 10-30. Lower Sindh (Hyderabad): March 1-20. Warmer climate leads to earlier maturity. Harvest promptly before hot weather causes shattering.

question: What is the correct harvesting time for linseed in KPK?
answer: KPK: April 15 to May 15. Peshawar valley: April 20-May 10. Dera Ismail Khan: April 10-30. Higher elevations (Swat): May 1-20. Later sowing and cooler climate shift harvest later.

question: What is the correct harvesting time for linseed in Balochistan?
answer: Balochistan: April to May. Quetta/Pishin: May 1-20. Sibi/Naseerabad (warm areas): April 10-30. Rainfed areas: harvest when capsules brown - depends on rains.

question: What post-harvest activities are done immediately after linseed harvest?
answer: 1) Drying: Spread in sun for 5-7 days until seeds rattle (8-10% moisture). 2) Threshing: Beating bundles or machine thresher. 3) Winnowing: Separate seeds from chaff using wind or fan. 4) Cleaning: Remove dust stones immature seeds. 5) Drying again: If moisture >10% - sun dry 1-2 more days. 6) Bagging: Clean jute/plastic bags. 7) Storage: Cool dry place.

question: How long after sowing is linseed typically harvested in Pakistan?
answer: 110-140 days after sowing depending on variety and season. Early varieties (LS-3): 110-120 days. Medium (LS-1 LS-2): 120-130 days. Late (R-17): 130-140 days. Rainfed conditions may extend by 5-10 days. Calculate backward from expected harvest to plan sowing.

question: What are the common mistakes farmers make during linseed harvesting in Pakistan?
answer: 1) Harvesting too early (green capsules) - immature seeds low oil content. 2) Harvesting too late (over-ripe) - shattering loss up to 30%. 3) Cutting too high - leaving lower capsules in field. 4) Rough handling - causes seed shattering. 5) Not drying properly - mold in storage. 6) Threshing on bare ground - mixing with soil/stones. 7) Using combine at wrong settings - cracked seeds. 8) Mixing varieties - inconsistent quality.

question: How should linseed be stored after harvest in Pakistan?
answer: 1) Dry seeds to 8-10% moisture (sun dry 5-7 days). 2) Clean thoroughly (remove weed seeds debris). 3) Store in clean dry jute bags or hermetic (PICS) bags. 4) Stack bags on wooden pallets (not direct floor). 5) Maintain cool dry well-ventilated store. 6) Treat with neem leaves or camphor for insects. 7) For long-term: fumigate with aluminum phosphide (2-3 tablets/ton) - use trained person. 8) Monitor monthly for moisture/pests.

question: What is the ideal moisture content of linseed for safe long-term storage?
answer: 8-10% moisture content for safe storage up to 12 months. Above 10%: risk of mold and heating. Above 12%: rapid deterioration. Below 8%: excessive brittleness and breakage. Use moisture meter for accuracy. Traditional test: bite seed - should be hard and crisp. Dry in sun if moisture high.

question: What are the major post-harvest losses for linseed in Pakistan and how to reduce them?
answer: Major losses: 1) Shattering during harvest (10-20%). Reduce: timely harvest gentle handling. 2) Incomplete threshing (5-10%). Reduce: proper threshing setting. 3) Bird damage (5-15% if left in field). Reduce: harvest promptly. 4) Storage insects (10-20% over 6 months). Reduce: dry seed proper storage fumigation. 5) Mold (5-15%). Reduce: dry to <10% moisture. Total losses can exceed 40% without proper management.

question: What storage structures or containers are recommended for linseed in rural Pakistan?
answer: 1) Metal bins (drum) - airtight rodent-proof best option. 2) Clay bins (Godaym) - traditional seal with mud. 3) Hermetic bags (PICS or GrainPro) - prevents insect entry no fumigation needed. 4) Jute bags (gunny) - with inner polythene liner. 5) Plastic silos (govt scheme). 6) Improved mud silo (PARC design). Avoid: direct floor storage old chemical bags damp rooms.

question: What pest control measures should be taken during linseed storage?
answer: 1) Clean storage area before filling. 2) Dry seed to 8-10% moisture. 3) Mix neem leaves (1kg/100kg seed) or dried neem powder. 4) Use food-grade diatomaceous earth (1kg/ton) - physical insecticide. 5) Fumigation: Aluminum phosphide tablets (2-3 per ton) - only by trained person. 6) Pheromone traps for monitoring. 7) Inspect monthly for webbing live insects musty smell. 8) Never mix old with new grain.

question: What fumigants or storage pesticides are recommended for linseed in Pakistan?
answer: 1) Aluminum phosphide (Phostoxin) - 2-3 tablets per ton. CAUTION: Highly toxic - use trained fumigator only. Seal storage for 5-7 days. Aerate 48 hours before use. 2) Malathion dust (2% active) - 250g per ton (mix with seed). 3) Deltamethrin dust - as label. For small quantities: neem leaves camphor (mothballs). Never consume treated seed for oil extraction.

question: How long can linseed be stored without significant quality loss?
answer: At 8-10% moisture in cool dry conditions: 12-18 months without significant quality loss (oil quality declines after 12 months). In hermetic bags: up to 24 months. In traditional jute bags: 6-12 months (depending on climate). In hot humid conditions: 3-6 months only. For seed purpose: use within 12 months for >80% germination.

question: How should linseed be dried before storage to prevent mold and fungal growth?
answer: 1) Sun drying: Spread on clean tarpaulin or cemented floor in thin layer (5-10 cm). 2) Turn every 2-3 hours for uniform drying. 3) Dry for 5-7 days (depending on sun). 4) Test moisture: Bite test (crisp) or moisture meter. 5) Do not dry on bare soil (contamination). 6) For large scale: mechanical dryers (hot air 40-45°C). 7) Cool seeds before bagging. Target 8-10% moisture.

question: What are the signs of spoilage or pest damage in stored linseed?
answer: Signs of spoilage: 1) Musty or sour smell (mold). 2) Clumping or caking (excess moisture). 3) Discolored seeds (dark brown black). 4) Sprouted seeds. 5) Heating (warm to touch). Pest damage: 1) Holes in seeds. 2) Fine dust/powder at bag bottom. 3) Webbing inside bag. 4) Live insects (weevils moths). 5) Empty seed hulls. Discard severely damaged seed.

question: What food safety practices should be followed during linseed storage and handling?
answer: 1) Never use pesticide-treated seed for oil extraction or consumption. 2) Do not store in containers that held chemicals/fertilizers. 3) Keep storage area clean and rodent-free. 4) Do not consume moldy seeds (may contain mycotoxins). 5) Wash hands after handling stored grain. 6) Use separate storage for seed vs. oilseed for consumption. 7) Follow PHI if field pesticides used. 8) For edible oil extraction use clean undamaged seeds.

question: How does frost (Quora) affect linseed and how can farmers protect it in Pakistan?
answer: Linseed is moderately frost tolerant at vegetative stage (down to -5°C). Frost at flowering (Feb) causes: 1) Flower drop (complete loss of that flush). 2) Damaged capsules (empty). 3) Stem cracking. Protection: 1) Sow at optimum time to avoid flowering during peak frost (Jan). 2) Irrigate before frost night (water releases heat). 3) Smoke: Burn moist crop residue upwind before dawn. 4) Use frost-tolerant varieties (LS-1).

question: How does extreme heat (above 40°C) affect linseed production in Pakistan?
answer: Linseed is cool-season crop. Heat above 35°C: 1) Reduces germination (if at sowing). 2) Accelerates maturity (shorter duration). 3) Reduces oil content (42% → 35%). 4) Causes flower abortion. 5) Small shriveled seeds. 6) Increases mite infestation. Avoid late sowing (Dec) that pushes grain filling into March-April heat. In Sindh/South Punjab: sow by Nov 15 maximum.

question: What are the drought-tolerant varieties of linseed recommended for rainfed areas of Pakistan?
answer: 1) LS-2 (NARC) - developed for rainfed Pothwar. 2) LS-3 (Barani Agricultural Research Chakwal) - early maturing escapes drought. 3) Local landraces from Chakwal/Attock - adapted over generations. 4) R-17 (Sindh) - drought + salt tolerance. These varieties have deeper roots earlier maturity and osmotic adjustment. Yield under rainfed: 6-8 maunds/acre vs 3-5 for non-adapted.

question: How should a farmer manage linseed during unexpected heavy rainfall or flooding?
answer: 1) Immediately stop any irrigation. 2) Ensure drainage: Open channels to remove standing water. 3) If waterlogging <24 hours: plants may recover. 4) If >48 hours: root rot likely - assess survival. 5) After water recedes: apply light N (urea 10-15 kg/acre) for recovery. 6) Monitor for fungal diseases (rust powdery mildew) - prophylactic fungicide spray. 7) For flooded young crop: may need replanting if early season.

question: What is the effect of fog or cloud cover on linseed growth in winter in Pakistan?
answer: Prolonged fog (Dec-Jan in Punjab): 1) Reduces photosynthesis (low light). 2) Increases humidity (promotes rust and powdery mildew). 3) Delays maturity. 4) Can cause etiolation (stretched weak stems). Management: 1) Wider row spacing (25-30 cm) for air circulation. 2) Preventive fungicide spray before fog period. 3) Avoid dense canopy (no excess N). 4) Use disease-resistant varieties.

question: How does hailstorm (Oola-bari) damage linseed and what can be done after hail?
answer: Hail damage: 1) Bruised stems (entry point for disease). 2) Shredded leaves. 3) Damaged capsules (seed loss). 4) Lodging (flattened crop). After hail: 1) Do not harvest immediately - wait 5-7 days for recovery assessment. 2) Apply fungicide (Mancozeb) to prevent infection through wounds. 3) Light N spray (1% urea) for recovery. 4) If >70% damage: consider alternative crop (if early season). 5) Report to agriculture department for possible compensation.

question: What heat-tolerant varieties of linseed are suitable for hot regions like Sindh and South Punjab?
answer: 1) LS-2 - moderate heat tolerance. 2) R-17 - developed for Sindh warmer conditions. 3) K-2 - traditional Sindh variety. 4) For South Punjab: LS-1 performs well if sown by Nov 15. Avoid LS-3 (early but small seeds). Key management: early sowing (Nov 1-15) to complete grain filling before March heat.

question: How should irrigation be adjusted for linseed during drought conditions in Pakistan?
answer: During drought: 1) Prioritize critical stages (branching flowering capsule filling) - irrigate these even if skip others. 2) Apply light irrigations (2-3 acre-inches) rather than heavy - less evaporation. 3) Use furrow irrigation (not flood) - more efficient. 4) Irrigate at night - less evaporation. 5) Mulch with crop residue (3-4 tons/acre) to conserve moisture. 6) If only 1 irrigation possible: apply at flowering (maximum yield response).

question: What climate-smart practices are recommended for linseed farmers in Pakistan?
answer: 1) Conservation agriculture: Zero-till/minimum till + residue retention (mulch). 2) Laser land leveling: Saves water improves uniformity. 3) Drought-tolerant varieties (LS-2). 4) Weather-based sowing decisions (use advisory services). 5) Micro-irrigation (drip/sprinkler) where feasible (60% subsidy). 6) Agroforestry: Trees on field boundaries reduce wind speed and evapotranspiration. 7) Crop diversification: Linseed in rotation with climate-resilient crops (millets sorghum).

question: What is the impact of late monsoon or early monsoon on linseed cultivation in Pakistan?
answer: Linseed is Rabi crop (sown Oct-Nov) so monsoon (Jul-Sep) does not directly affect growing crop. However: Late monsoon (rains extending into Oct) delays land preparation and sowing - causes late sowing yield loss. Early monsoon (starting Apr) can damage mature crop (Mar-Apr harvest) causing sprouting in capsules and shattering. Monitor forecasts and harvest promptly if early rains expected.

Contact provincial agriculture department.

question: Which research institutes in Pakistan have developed improved linseed varieties?
answer: 1) Ayub Agricultural Research Institute (AARI) Faisalabad - developed LS-1. 2) National Agricultural Research Centre (NARC) Islamabad - developed LS-2. 3) Barani Agricultural Research Institute (BARI) Chakwal - developed LS-3. 4) Oilseed Research Program NARC - general linseed improvement. 5) Sindh Agriculture University Tandojam - R-17 and K-2. 6) Pakistan Agricultural Research Council (PARC) - coordination.

question: Where can farmers in Pakistan get certified linseed seed?
answer: 1) Punjab Seed Corporation (PSC) - regional offices in Faisalabad Multan Lahore. 2) Provincial Agriculture Department extension centers. 3) Ayub Agricultural Research Institute Faisalabad (direct sale). 4) NARC Islamabad (for LS-2). 5) Barani Agricultural Research Chakwal (for LS-3). 6) Progressive seed dealers (check certification tag). 7) Sindh Seed Corporation (for R-17). Price: Rs. 100-150/kg. Demand certified seed early (Aug-Oct) as limited quantity.

question: What extension services are available for linseed farmers in Pakistan?
answer: 1) Agriculture Department field staff (Agriculture Officers Field Assistants) - free advice. 2) Kisan Helpline 0800-15000 (Punjab) for queries. 3) SMS advisory services (CropMax Punjab) - weather pest alerts. 4) Farmer field schools (FFS) - hands-on training. 5) Agriculture extension WhatsApp groups (district level). 6) Mobile apps: "Agriculture Punjab" "Kisan Dost". 7) Radio/TV programs (Zaraat Nama on PBC). 8) Demonstration plots at union council level.

Requirements: land ownership/lease record CNIC. Loan covers seed fertilizer pesticides. Repay after harvest.

question: What agricultural insurance is available for linseed crops in Pakistan?
answer: 1) PM Crop Insurance Scheme (under Kisan Package) - covers linseed. 2) Premium: 3-5% of sum insured (farmer pays 50% govt subsidy 50%). 3) Coverage: Yield loss >30% due to drought flood hail pests. 4) Claim: Rs. 20
column6: 000/acre depending on coverage. 5) Providers: State Life Insurance Takaful Pakistan. Enrollment before sowing (Oct-Nov). Contact agriculture department for Kisan Card insurance component.

question: Where can a farmer in Pakistan report disease outbreaks or pest attacks on linseed?
answer: 1) District Agriculture Office (Extension) - immediate reporting. 2) Plant Protection Department - for locusts/quarantine pests. 3) Kisan Helpline 0800-15000 (Punjab). 4) Agriculture Complaint Cell 0800-30000. 5) Local Agriculture Field Assistant (FA) - village level. 6) WhatsApp groups of agriculture department. 7) Crop Reporting Centre (for statistics). For rust outbreak: report early so advisory can be issued.

question: What role does the Provincial Agriculture Department play in supporting linseed farmers?
answer: 1) Provide extension services (field visits training). 2) Distribute subsidized inputs (seed fertilizer). 3) Soil testing facilities (free/low cost). 4) Pest/disease forecasting and alerts. 5) Subsidy administration (Kisan Card drip irrigation). 6) Organize farmer field days and demonstrations. 7) Link farmers with credit and insurance. 8) Research linkage (recommend improved varieties). 9) Market information and price updates. Contact Provincial Director Agriculture (extension wing).

question: What is matter (green peas) and what is its agricultural importance in Pakistan?
answer: Matter (green peas - Pisum sativum) known as Matar is an important rabi vegetable and pulse crop in Pakistan. Its agricultural importance includes: 1) Fresh green peas for vegetable market (high value Rs. 80-150/kg). 2) Dried peas (mature) for dal and pulse flour. 3) Nitrogen fixation (60-80 kg N/ha) improves soil fertility. 4) Short duration (90-110 days) fits in multiple cropping systems. 5) High protein content (20-25%) for nutrition. 6) Fodder for livestock after pod harvest.

question: What are the main growing regions of matter (green peas) in Pakistan?
answer: Matter is grown throughout Pakistan but major regions: Punjab: Okara Sahiwal Sialkot Gujranwala Lahore Kasur Sheikhupura Nankana Sahib and rainfed Pothwar (Rawalpindi Attock Chakwal). Sindh: Hyderabad Mirpurkhas Sukkur and Tando Allahyar. KPK: Peshawar Mardan Swat Abbottabad Mansehra. Balochistan: Quetta Pishin Kalat Mastung (spring/summer crop). Gilgit-Baltistan and Kashmir (summer).

question: What are the climate and temperature requirements for successful cultivation of matter in Pakistan?
answer: Matter requires cool temperate climate. Optimum temperature: 15-20°C for vegetative growth, 12-18°C for pod formation. Minimum for germination: 5-7°C. Maximum tolerance: 28°C (above this stops flowering and pod set). Frost at flowering (>-3°C) damages flowers. Requires 400-600mm rainfall or irrigation. Dry weather during harvest essential.

question: In which season(s) is matter cultivated in Pakistan (Rabi/Kharif)?
answer: Matter is primarily a Rabi (winter) crop in plains of Pakistan sown October-November and harvested January-March. In high altitude areas (Balochistan KPK hills Gilgit) it is grown as a spring/summer crop (Kharif) sown March-May and harvested June-August. Some areas have off-season cultivation in August-September using tunnels.

question: What is the typical crop duration/life cycle of matter from sowing to harvest?
answer: Typical crop duration is 80-120 days depending on variety and climate. Early varieties: 65-75 days. Medium varieties: 80-95 days. Late varieties: 100-120 days. In warm plains: shorter duration (70-90 days). In cool highlands: longer duration (100-120 days).

question: What are the growth stages of matter and what happens at each stage?
answer: 1) Germination (0-10 days): Seed absorbs water radicle emerges at 5-10°C. 2) Seedling (10-20 days): First true leaves root development. 3) Vegetative growth (20-45 days): Stem elongation tendrils branching. 4) Flowering (45-65 days): White/pink flowers open for 10-15 days. 5) Pod formation (55-80 days): Pods develop fill with peas. 6) Maturity (80-120 days): Pods turn yellow-brown peas harden. 7) Harvest (green): At 70-80% pod fill.

question: How does matter contribute to food security and the farming economy in Pakistan?
answer: Matter contributes significantly: 1) Provides affordable protein-rich vegetable (Rs. 80-150/kg) for urban/rural populations. 2) Generates income for small farmers (Rs. 150,000-300,000/acre profit). 3) Nitrogen fixation reduces fertilizer need for subsequent crops (wheat). 4) Short duration allows double cropping (pea-wheat or pea-rice). 5) Export potential to Middle East (fresh and frozen). 6) Processing industry (frozen peas canning). 7) Employment during harvesting (20-30 laborers/acre).

question: How should land be prepared before sowing matter in Pakistan?
answer: Land should be prepared to fine tilth (seedbed). Sequence: 1) Deep ploughing with disc plough (if hardpan present). 2) 2-3 cultivations with cultivator. 3) Planking after each cultivation. 4) Laser leveling for uniform moisture. 5) Final planking just before sowing. For heavy soils: add 1-2 more cultivations and make raised beds.

question: How many ploughings are recommended for land preparation for matter?
answer: 4-6 ploughings/tillage passes: 1 deep ploughing (every 2-3 years) + 2-3 cultivator passes + 1-2 plankings. In heavy clay soils: 5-6 passes. In sandy soils: 3-4 passes. Each pass at different angles. Fine seedbed is critical for small seeds.

question: What is the role of deep ploughing in matter cultivation?
answer: Deep ploughing (25-30 cm) with disc plough: 1) Breaks hardpan and improves root penetration (roots go 60-90 cm). 2) Enhances water infiltration and drainage (critical for matter). 3) Exposes soil pests to predators. 4) Incorporates crop residues and organic matter. 5) Reduces weed seed bank. Do once every 2-3 years.

question: What is the recommended land leveling (Laser Leveling) method before planting matter?
answer: Laser leveling is highly recommended. Benefits: 1) Uniform irrigation (prevents waterlogging in low spots). 2) Saves 20-30% irrigation water. 3) Improves germination uniformity. 4) Reduces weed patches. Field leveled to ±1 cm variation. Service cost: Rs. 2,000-3,000/acre. Subsidy available through Agriculture Department.

question: Should ridges and furrows be made for matter cultivation in Pakistan? How?
answer: Ridges and furrows (raised beds) are highly recommended especially for heavy soils and winter rainfall areas. Method: 1) Make 45-60 cm wide beds. 2) Sow 2 rows on each bed (30-45 cm apart). 3) Furrow depth 15-20 cm. Benefits: prevents waterlogging improves drainage reduces root rot and makes harvesting easier. Essential in clay soils.

question: How should previously harvested crop residue be managed before planting matter?
answer: 1) If previous crop was cereal (wheat rice maize): incorporate stubble by shallow ploughing. 2) Avoid planting matter after other legumes (gram lentil beans) - minimum 3-4 year rotation. 3) Remove or deeply bury pea residues after harvest (disease carryover). 4) For rice stubble: manage with disc harrow + cultivator. 5) Do not burn residue - incorporate for organic matter.

question: What pre-sowing irrigation (Raunni) is required for matter land preparation?
answer: Pre-sowing irrigation (raunni) given 15-20 days before sowing when soil moisture is low. Apply 3-4 acre-inches water. After irrigation: allow soil to reach field capacity then cultivate when moisture at "good tilth" (soil crumbles but does not stick). Saves 1-2 irrigations during crop growth. Essential for rainfed areas.

question: What implements and machinery are used for land preparation for matter in Pakistan?
answer: 1) Disc plough (deep ploughing). 2) Cultivator (2-3 passes). 3) Disc harrow (clod breaking in heavy soils). 4) Rotavator (fine seedbed - use moderately). 5) Plank (leveling and moisture conservation). 6) Laser land leveler. 7) Ridger/bed planter (for raised beds). 8) Rotary tiller (for seedbed).

question: How many days before sowing should land preparation begin for matter?
answer: Start land preparation 15-20 days before sowing. Timeline: Day 1: deep ploughing (if needed). Day 2-5: first cultivation + planking. Day 7-10: second cultivation + planking. Day 12-14: pre-sowing irrigation (if needed). Day 15-18: final cultivation + planking + bed making. Day 18-20: sowing.

question: How does land preparation differ for irrigated vs. rainfed (Barani) matter cultivation?
answer: Irrigated: finer seedbed required, laser leveling important, ridges for heavy soils, pre-sowing irrigation optional. Rainfed (Barani): focus on moisture conservation - fewer cultivations (3-4 passes), deep ploughing for water storage, no pre-sowing irrigation (preserve soil moisture), rougher seedbed to reduce evaporation, mulching with crop residue. Also use drought-tolerant varieties.

question: What is the recommended seed rate (kg/acre) for matter in Pakistan?
answer: Recommended seed rate: 40-50 kg/acre for fresh green pea production. For dried peas (dal): 35-40 kg/acre. For rainfed areas: 50-60 kg/acre (compensates for poor germination). For small-seeded varieties: 35-40 kg/acre. For bold-seeded varieties: 45-55 kg/acre. Seed treatment essential.

question: What is the optimum row spacing and plant spacing for matter in Pakistan?
answer: Row spacing: 30-45 cm (12-18 inches). For bush varieties: 30 cm. For climbing/tall varieties: 45 cm. Plant to plant spacing: 5-10 cm after thinning. On beds: 2 rows per bed (45 cm bed). Target plant population: 250,000-300,000 plants per acre. Closer spacing for green peas (higher pod density).

question: What is the recommended sowing depth for matter seeds in Pakistan?
answer: Sowing depth: 3-5 cm (1.5-2 inches). In sandy soils: 5-6 cm. In heavy soils: 2-3 cm. Deeper than 6 cm reduces emergence. Shallower than 2 cm risks drying out or bird damage. Seed should be placed in moist soil but not too deep. Cover with soil and light planking.

question: What sowing method is best for matter — broadcast (Chatha) drill dibbling or transplanting?
answer: Drill sowing is best: 1) Uniform depth and spacing. 2) Seed saving (20-30% less seed). 3) Better germination. 4) Easier weed control. 5) Higher yield (15-20% more). 6) Good for mechanized harvesting. Broadcasting (chatha) is traditional but inefficient. Dibbling is labor intensive. Transplanting not practiced for peas.

question: How should matter be sown after a previous crop (e.g. rice-wheat or cotton-wheat system)?
answer: 1) After rice: Use zero-till drill to sow peas into rice stubble. Allow 7-10 days for field to dry after rice harvest. 2) After cotton/wheat: Conventional tillage with 2-3 cultivations. 3) Ensure no herbicide carryover (pendimethalin from rice/wheat can damage peas - check labels). 4) In rice-wheat system peas can be relay cropped 10-15 days before wheat harvest. 5) Matter after maize: excellent rotation.

question: Can matter be sown using zero-till or minimum-till techniques in Pakistan?
answer: Yes zero-till is successful for matter especially after rice. Benefits: 1) Saves 15-20 days and Rs. 3,000-4,000/acre land prep. 2) Moisture conservation. 3) Earlier sowing by 10-15 days. 4) Reduced weed pressure. Use zero-till drill with inverted T-type furrow opener. Seed rate: increase by 10-15% (45-55 kg/acre). Apply pre-emergence herbicide.

question: What equipment or tools (Seed Drill Planter) are used for sowing matter in Pakistan?
answer: 1) Conventional seed drill (most common) - 9-11 row. 2) Zero-till drill (for after rice). 3) Bed planter (for ridge sowing). 4) Vegetable planter (precision). 5) Manual dibbler (small farms). 6) Pora (traditional wooden drill). Calibrate drill for 40-50 kg/acre seed rate. Row spacing 30-45 cm.

question: What are all the major crop management activities for matter from sowing to harvest?
answer: Timeline: 0-10 days: sowing seed treatment. 10-20 days: germination check gap filling first irrigation. 20-30 days: first weeding inter-cultivation Rhizobium nodulation check. 30-40 days: second weeding vegetative growth. 40-50 days: flowering stage - irrigation pest monitoring (aphids). 50-65 days: pod formation - second irrigation disease monitoring (powdery mildew). 65-80 days: pod filling - late irrigation if needed. 80-100 days: harvest (green or dry).

question: What is the complete activity calendar (timeline) for matter cultivation in Pakistan?
answer: October: land preparation (15-30 Oct). November: sowing (1-20 Nov). November-December: germination emergence gap filling (15 Nov-10 Dec) first irrigation (20-30 Nov). December: first weeding (1-15 Dec) inter-cultivation (15-31 Dec). January: second weeding (1-15 Jan) flowering (15-31 Jan) irrigation. February: pod formation (1-20 Feb) pest/disease monitoring. March: pod filling (1-15 Mar) late irrigation. March-April: harvest green (15 Mar-15 Apr) or dry (Apr).

question: When should thinning (Gidai) be done in matter cultivation and how?
answer: Thinning at 15-20 days after sowing when plants are 8-10 cm tall. Method: 1) Remove excess plants to achieve spacing 5-10 cm between plants. 2) Keep healthier vigorous plants. 3) Remove weak diseased and damaged seedlings. 4) Do not disturb roots of retained plants. 5) Irrigate lightly after thinning. Target population: 250
column6: 000 plants/acre. Overcrowding leads to poor air circulation and disease.

question: When should earthing up (Mitti charhana) be done for matter and why?
answer: Earthing up is generally not required for bush pea varieties. For climbing/tall varieties: light earthing up at 25-30 days. Method: pull soil around base of plants (5-10 cm high). Benefits: 1) Supports stems (reduces lodging). 2) Covers weeds. 3) Improves drainage. 4) Provides support for trellising (if used). Not practiced for bush peas.

question: How should inter-cultivation (Godi) be done in matter fields?
answer: Inter-cultivation at 25-30 days and 40-45 days after sowing. Method: 1) Use hand hoe (khurpa) or wheel hoe. 2) Cultivate between rows at 5-8 cm depth. 3) Avoid damaging plant roots. 4) Also breaks soil crust removes weeds aerates soil. 5) Bring soil slightly toward plants (light earthing). For large areas: use cultivator with adjustable tines set to avoid plants.

question: What is the process of transplanting matter seedlings (if applicable) and when should it be done?
answer: Transplanting is NOT practiced for peas in Pakistan. Peas are always direct seeded due to: 1) Sensitive taproot - transplanting shock reduces yield. 2) Short growing season. 3) Higher cost not justified. Use direct seeding only.

question: What is the optimal plant population per acre for matter in Pakistan?
answer: Optimal plant population: 250
column6: 000 plants per acre (60-75 plants per square meter). For bush varieties: 280
column10: 000 plants/acre (more space needed). Achieve by: seed rate 40-50 kg/acre + thinning. Higher population causes lodging and more disease (powdery mildew). Lower population reduces yield.

question: How is gap filling done in matter cultivation if germination is poor?
answer: Gap filling at 10-15 days after sowing. Method: 1) Pre-soak seeds for 4-6 hours (for gap filling only). 2) Dibble 2-3 seeds per gap (missing plant area). 3) After emergence thin to 1-2 plants per gap. 4) Irrigate lightly after gap filling. 5) If gaps >30%: consider replanting (if early enough). Use same variety as original sowing.

question: When and how should staking or support be provided to matter plants?
answer: Staking is needed for climbing/tall varieties (e.g. Rando Climax). Method: 1) Install bamboo stakes or wooden poles at row ends. 2) Stretch twine or plastic netting between poles (30-40 cm above ground). 3) Provide second tier at 60-70 cm. 4) For bush varieties (Meteor Peas-2009): no staking needed - they are self-supporting (30-45 cm tall). Staking improves air circulation and pod quality.

question: What is pinching or pruning in matter and when should it be done?
answer: Pinching (removal of apical meristem) is NOT recommended for peas. It reduces yield and delays maturity. Peas naturally stop growing after flowering. Some growers remove lower leaves at 40 days to improve air circulation (reduces mildew) - but not standard practice.

question: How should matter be managed during flowering to maximize fruit/grain set?
answer: 1) Ensure adequate soil moisture (irrigate if dry). 2) Avoid pesticide sprays during peak flowering (9 AM-4 PM) to protect bees and natural pollinators. 3) Provide boron (foliar 0.1% boric acid) at bud stage if deficient. 4) Protect from frost (irrigation before frost night or smoke). 5) Manage aphids (honeydew interferes with pollination). 6) Avoid overhead irrigation which washes pollen. 7) Provide support for tall varieties.

question: What is the process of ratooning (Munda) for matter in Pakistan? Is it recommended?
answer: Ratooning is NOT recommended for peas. Unlike sugarcane peas do not regrow after harvest. Secondary growth is poor low yielding and disease-prone. Always plant fresh seed each season. For multiple harvests: plant early varieties in succession (every 15 days).

question: How does crop canopy management improve yield of matter?
answer: Canopy management: 1) Optimum plant population (250
column6: 000 plants/acre) prevents overcrowding. 2) Proper row spacing (30-45 cm) allows light penetration and air circulation. 3) Avoid excess N which causes dense canopy and powdery mildew. 4) Inter-cultivation improves air circulation reducing disease. 5) For tall varieties: staking keeps canopy open. Good canopy = healthy plants + high pod yield.

question: What field monitoring activities should a farmer do weekly during matter season?
answer: Weekly monitoring: 1) Germination % (first 2 weeks). 2) Plant stand and gaps. 3) Nodulation check (dig up roots - look for pink nodules at 30 days). 4) Weed presence and type. 5) Pest scouting: aphids (check young shoots and flowers) whitefly thrips. 6) Disease signs: powdery mildew (white powder on leaves) rust (orange pustules) root rot (yellowing). 7) Nutrient deficiency symptoms. 8) Soil moisture. Record observations.

question: What are the most commonly grown varieties of matter (green peas) in Pakistan?
answer: Commonly grown varieties include: 1) Climax (medium maturity high yield). 2) Meteor (early maturing 65-70 days). 3) Green King (dark green pods). 4) Rando (late maturing for high hills). 5) Local Desi (small seeded drought tolerant). 6) Peas 2009 (Ayub Research). 7) Spring Pea (for KPK and Balochistan). Traditional varieties are low-yielding (30-40 maunds/acre).

question: What are the improved and recommended varieties of matter approved by Pakistani agricultural research institutes?
answer: Improved varieties approved by PARC/NARC/Ayub Research: 1) Peas-2009 (Ayub Research Faisalabad) - high yield 60-70 maunds/acre early maturing 80 days powdery mildew tolerant. 2) Meteor (NARC) - very early 65-70 days for plains. 3) Climax (AARI) - medium 85-90 days high pod yield. 4) Green King (Vegetable Research Institute Sahiwal) - dark green export quality. 5) Rando (for high altitude). 6) PF-400 (Peshawar). 7) Samrina Zard (yellow seeded for dal).

question: What are the early-maturing medium-maturing and late-maturing varieties of matter available in Pakistan?
answer: Early-maturing (65-75 days): Meteor, Peas-2009, Early Badger. Medium-maturing (80-95 days): Climax, Green King, PF-400. Late-maturing (100-120 days): Rando, Local Desi (hills), Spring Pea (for cool summers). Early varieties suitable for plains and double cropping. Late varieties for high altitudes (Balochistan, KPK hills, Gilgit).

question: What type of soil is best suited for growing matter in Pakistan?
answer: Well-drained loamy or sandy loam soil rich in organic matter is best. Deep fertile soils (45-60 cm depth) with pH 6.0-7.5. Avoid heavy clays (poor drainage) and very sandy soils (low water holding). Matter is sensitive to waterlogging. Ideal soil has good aeration for nodulation.

question: What is the ideal soil pH range for matter cultivation in Pakistan?
answer: Ideal pH range is 6.0 to 7.5 (slightly acidic to neutral). Matter can tolerate pH 5.5-8.0 but yields decline below 5.5 (aluminum toxicity) and above 8.0 (iron and manganese deficiency). At high pH >7.5: Rhizobium bacteria activity reduced - fix less nitrogen.

question: What soil texture (loamy sandy clayey) is most suitable for matter?
answer: Sandy loam and loam are most suitable - provide good drainage aeration and root penetration. Sandy soils: require frequent irrigation and organic matter addition. Clayey soils: problematic due to poor drainage (root rot) and crusting (poor emergence). Silty loam is also good.

question: Can matter be grown on saline or sodic soils (Kallar) in Pakistan? What are the precautions?
answer: Matter is salt-sensitive (ECe <2 dS/m). Not recommended on saline or sodic soils. If unavoidable: 1) Apply gypsum at 100% GR. 2) Heavy leaching before sowing. 3) Use raised beds. 4) Add FYM 15-20 tons/acre. 5) Use salt-tolerant varieties (none specifically for matter). 6) Better to avoid - choose salt-tolerant crops like barley or sugarbeet.

question: What soil drainage conditions are required for matter?
answer: Excellent drainage is critical. Matter is highly sensitive to waterlogging - even 24-48 hours of standing water causes root death yellowing and plant death. Raised beds (30-45 cm high) essential in heavy soils or high rainfall areas. Good drainage also prevents root rot diseases.

question: How does soil organic matter content affect the yield of matter?
answer: Higher organic matter (1.5-3%) improves: 1) Water holding capacity. 2) Nutrient availability (especially N P S). 3) Soil structure and root penetration. 4) Beneficial Rhizobium bacteria activity (better nodulation). 5) Drought tolerance. Every 0.5% increase in OM can boost yield by 2-4 maunds/acre.

question: What soil testing should a farmer do before planting matter in Pakistan?
answer: Essential soil tests: 1) pH and EC (salinity). 2) Organic matter. 3) Available P (Olsen P) - critical for pea. 4) Available K. 5) Micronutrients: Boron (B) and Zinc (Zn) for sandy/alkaline soils. 6) Soil texture. 7) Previous crop (avoid after other legumes). Sample depth: 6-9 inches. Send to provincial soil testing lab (free or low cost).

question: How should soil fertility be maintained or improved for repeated cultivation of matter?
answer: 1) Crop rotation: matter after cereals (wheat maize) - not after other legumes (gram lentil) to avoid disease buildup. 2) Apply FYM/compost 10-15 tons/acre every 2-3 years. 3) Green manuring before matter. 4) Balanced P and K fertilization (no N needed due to fixation). 5) Inoculate seed with Rhizobium bacteria. 6) Incorporate crop residues (not pea residues).

question: What are the signs of poor or unsuitable soil for matter cultivation?
answer: Signs: 1) Water pooling after rain/irrigation (poor drainage). 2) White salt crust (saline). 3) Stunted yellow plants (N deficiency or waterlogging). 4) Poor nodulation (no pink nodules on roots - low Rhizobia). 5) Cracked clay soil surface. 6) Poor germination and seedling death (soil crusting or salinity).

question: What soil preparation practices improve the structure and health of soil for matter?
answer: 1) Deep ploughing (25-30 cm) every 2-3 years. 2) Add organic matter (FYM 10-15 tons/acre). 3) Green manuring 6-8 weeks before sowing. 4) Gypsum application for sodic soils. 5) Laser leveling for uniform irrigation and drainage. 6) Avoid excessive tillage which destroys soil structure. 7) Raised bed preparation for heavy soils.

question: When is the best time to sow matter in Punjab Pakistan?
answer: Optimum sowing: October 15 to November 15. North/Central Punjab (Lahore Faisalabad Gujranwala): Oct 20-Nov 10. South Punjab (Multan Bahawalpur): Nov 1-20. Early sowing (Oct) risks high temperature poor germination. Late sowing (Dec) reduces yield due to heat during pod filling. Rainfed areas: Oct 15-30.

question: When is the best time to sow matter in Sindh Pakistan?
answer: Sindh: October 15 to November 30. Upper Sindh (Sukkur Jacobabad): Oct 25-Nov 15. Lower Sindh (Hyderabad Mirpurkhas): Nov 1-30. Warmer climate allows later sowing. Avoid December sowing as high temperatures during pod development reduce quality. For spring crop in cooler areas: Jan-Feb.

question: When is the best time to sow matter in KPK Pakistan?
answer: KPK: October 1 to November 15. Peshawar valley: Oct 15-Nov 15. Dera Ismail Khan: Nov 1-20. Higher elevations (Swat Abbottabad Mansehra): March-April (spring crop) - sow when frost risk passes. Use cold-tolerant varieties for late sowing. Spring crop harvest June-July.

question: When is the best time to sow matter in Balochistan Pakistan?
answer: Balochistan: Two seasons. Plains (Sibi Naseerabad): Oct 15-Nov 30 (winter crop). Highlands (Quetta Pishin Kalat): March-April (spring crop) - sow after last frost (mid-March). Summer crop in high valleys: May-June. Use appropriate varieties for each season (early for spring).

question: When is the best time to sow matter in South Punjab (Multan Bahawalpur DG Khan)?
answer: South Punjab: November 1 to November 20. Warmer winter allows later sowing. Sow by Nov 20 maximum. Delay to December reduces yield 1-2% per day due to heat stress. Heat-tolerant varieties recommended. For early market: sow Oct 25-Nov 5.

question: What happens if matter is sown too early or too late in Pakistan?
answer: Too early (September-early October): 1) High temperatures (>30°C) reduce germination. 2) Vegetative growth excessive. 3) Flowering in warm weather - poor pod set. 4) More pest pressure (aphids). Too late (December onward): 1) Shortened growing season. 2) Heat stress during pod filling - small shriveled peas. 3) Lower yield (40-60% loss). 4) Poor quality (tough fibrous pods).

question: How does sowing time affect the yield and quality of matter?
answer: Yield: Each week delay after Nov 15 reduces yield by 5-10%. Optimum Nov sowing gives 60-80 maunds/acre. December sowing gives 30-40 maunds. Quality: Late sowing produces small tough peas with lower sugar content (less sweet). Early sowing (Oct) may give good yield but risk of frost damage at flowering in northern areas.

question: What seed treatment (Zahar-alood) should be done before sowing matter in Pakistan?
answer: Seed treatment is essential for matter: 1) Rhizobium inoculation (for nitrogen fixation). 2) Fungicide for seed-borne diseases (Fusarium Pythium). 3) Insecticide for early pests. 4) Micronutrient coating (optional). Treat seeds 24-48 hours before sowing. Use 20-30 ml water per kg seed for uniform coating.

question: Which fungicide is recommended for seed treatment of matter to prevent soil-borne diseases?
answer: Recommended fungicides: 1) Carbendazim (Bavistin) 2g per kg seed. 2) Thiram 2.5g per kg seed. 3) Captan 2g per kg. 4) Metalaxyl (Apron) 2g per kg - effective against Pythium and Phytophthora. 5) Tebuconazole (Raxil) 1.5ml per kg. These control seed-borne Fusarium wilt and root rot. For severe disease history: double the dose.

question: Which insecticide is recommended for seed treatment of matter to protect against early pests?
answer: 1) Imidacloprid (Confidor) 5ml per kg seed - controls early aphids and thrips up to 30 days. 2) Chlorpyrifos 2-3ml per kg - for termites. 3) Thiamethoxam (Cruiser) 4ml per kg - broad spectrum. 4) Carbofuran (Furadan) 3G 5g per kg - for soil pests (highly toxic - handle with care). For termite-prone areas use chlorpyrifos.

question: What is the process of seed treatment for matter — dose method and timing?
answer: Process: 1) Calculate seed quantity (40-50 kg/acre). 2) Mix required fungicide + insecticide + Rhizobium in 200-300ml water per kg seed (for Rhizobium use jaggery solution). 3) Spread seeds on clean polythene sheet. 4) Pour solution gradually while mixing manually (wear gloves). 5) Ensure uniform coating. 6) Dry in shade for 1-2 hours (not direct sun). 7) Sow within 24-48 hours.

question: Should matter seeds be soaked in water before sowing? For how long?
answer: Soaking is NOT recommended for peas. Soaked seeds: 1) Swell and become soft - prone to breakage during drilling. 2) Rot in cold wet soil. 3) Attract birds and rodents. 4) Lose vigor if not sown immediately. Dry seed treatment followed by direct sowing is best.

question: How does seed treatment affect germination rate and early growth of matter?
answer: Seed treatment increases germination from 60-70% (untreated) to 85-95% (treated). Rhizobium inoculation: 1) Forms nodules on roots (visible pink nodules at 30-40 days). 2) Fixes 60-80 kg N per acre. 3) Reduces N fertilizer need by 100%. 4) Dark green leaves and vigorous growth. Fungicide protects from damping off. Result: 20-30% higher yield potential.

question: What is bio-priming or microbial seed treatment for matter in Pakistan?
answer: Bio-priming involves treating seeds with beneficial microbes: 1) Rhizobium leguminosarum (specific for peas) - 1 packet (500g) for 20-25 kg seed. 2) PSB (Phosphorus Solubilizing Bacteria) - 1 packet for 10 kg seed. 3) Trichoderma harzianum (bio-fungicide) - 5g per kg seed. Mix with jaggery solution (50g jaggery in 1L water) as adhesive. Dry in shade. Reduces chemical fertilizer need by 25-50%.

question: How should treated matter seed be stored before sowing?
answer: Treated seeds should be sown within 24-48 hours maximum. Do not store treated seeds for more than 7 days as fungicides degrade and Rhizobia die. If storage unavoidable: keep in cool dry place (10-15°C) in breathable (not plastic) bags. Never mix treated seeds with untreated seeds. Rhizobium-treated seeds are especially sensitive to heat.

question: What are the safety precautions when doing seed treatment for matter?
answer: 1) Wear gloves and mask. 2) Do not eat/drink during treatment. 3) Treat in well-ventilated area. 4) Wash hands thoroughly after treatment. 5) Keep treated seed away from children and livestock. 6) Dispose empty chemical containers properly (triple rinse then crush). 7) Do not use treated seed for consumption. 8) Store chemicals separately.

question: What are the major weeds (Khar-palwar) found in matter fields in Pakistan?
answer: Major weeds: Broadleaf: 1) Bathu (Chenopodium album). 2) Maina (Asphodelus tenuifolius). 3) Peeli Buti (Fumaria parviflora). 4) Lehli (Sonchus asper). 5) Jangli palak (Rumex dentatus). 6) Kandiar (Convolvulus arvensis). Grasses: 1) Wild oat (Avena fatua) - most problematic. 2) Phalaris minor (Dumbi sitti). 3) Cyperus rotundus (Deela). 4) Cynodon dactylon (Khabbal grass)."

question: What is the critical period of weed competition in matter cultivation?
answer: Critical period: 15 to 50 days after sowing (from seedling to flowering). Weeds competing during this period cause 50-80% yield loss. First 30 days are most critical. Keep weed-free during this window. After 50 days pea canopy closes and suppresses late weeds.

question: How does weed competition affect the yield of matter in Pakistan?
answer: Weed competition can reduce yield by 50-80%. Heavy infestation: yield drop from 70 maunds to 15-20 maunds/acre. Grassy weeds (wild oat) are more damaging than broadleaf. Weeds compete for: water (critical in rainfed) nutrients (especially N) light and space. Also harbor pests (aphids) and increase humidity (powdery mildew).

question: What are the recommended herbicides (Zahar) for weed control in matter in Pakistan?
answer: 1) Pre-emergence: Pendimethalin (Stomp) 500-600ml/acre or Trifluralin (Treflan) 400-500ml/acre. 2) Pre-plant incorporated: Trifluralin. 3) Post-emergence (broadleaf): MCPA 300-400ml/acre (apply before flowering). 4) Post-emergence (grasses): Quizalofop (Topik) 300ml/acre or Fenoxaprop (Puma) 400ml/acre. DO NOT use 2
soil: 4-D on peas - severe damage (leaf curling pod malformation).

question: What pre-emergence herbicides are used for matter weed control?
answer: Pre-emergence (apply within 3 days of sowing before weed emergence): 1) Pendimethalin (Stomp) 500-600 ml/acre - effective on grasses and small-seeded broadleaf weeds. 2) Trifluralin (Treflan) 400-500 ml/acre - incorporate into top 5-8 cm soil within 24 hours. 3) Linuron 300-400g/acre - for broadleaf weeds. Apply on moist soil. Do not use on sandy soils (leaching risk).

question: What post-emergence herbicides are used for matter weed control?
answer: Post-emergence (apply at 20-30 days after sowing before flowering): For broadleaf weeds: MCPA 300-400 ml/acre at 3-5 leaf stage of weeds. For grassy weeds: Quizalofop ethyl (Topik) 300ml/acre or Fenoxaprop (Puma) 400ml/acre. DO NOT use 2
soil: 4-D (causes severe pod distortion). Do not spray after bud formation (45 days) as it may affect flowers and pods.

question: What is the correct dose and timing of herbicide application in matter?
answer: Pendimethalin: 500-600 ml/acre within 3 days of sowing. MCPA: 300-400 ml/acre at 20-30 days (weed 3-5 leaf). Quizalofop: 300ml/acre at 20-30 days for grass weeds. Use 100-120 liters water/acre. Flat fan nozzle. Apply in morning when no wind/rain. Do not spray after flowering.

question: How should manual weeding (Khurpa/Godi) be done in matter fields?
answer: Manual weeding: 1st weeding at 20-25 days (after thinning). 2nd weeding at 40-45 days (before flowering). Method: 1) Use khurpa (hand hoe) to cut weeds just below soil surface. 2) Remove weeds from field (don't leave uprooted weeds). 3) Be careful not to disturb pea roots and nodules. 4) Weeding also aerates soil. Labor requirement: 20-30 person-days/acre for two weedings.

question: How many manual weedings are recommended for matter cultivation in Pakistan?
answer: Two manual weedings are recommended: 1st at 20-25 days after sowing. 2nd at 40-45 days after sowing. In low weed pressure areas: one weeding at 25-30 days may suffice. In heavy weed infestation: two weedings + pre-emergence herbicide. Rainfed areas: timely weeding critical due to limited moisture.

question: What mechanical methods (Weeders) can be used for weed control in matter?
answer: 1) Wheel hoe (hand-operated) - for row spacing 30-45 cm. 2) Tractor-drawn cultivator with adjustable tines - for large fields (set to avoid plant rows). 3) Cono-weeder (for narrow rows). Mechanical weeding at 25-30 and 40-45 days. Inter-cultivation should be shallow (5-8 cm) to avoid root damage. Followed by manual removal of intra-row weeds.

question: How can mulching help control weeds in matter cultivation?
answer: Mulching is effective for peas: 1) Straw mulch (wheat/rice) at 3-4 tons/acre applied after sowing suppresses weeds. 2) Reduces weed germination by blocking light. 3) Also conserves soil moisture (valuable for rainfed). 4) Plastic mulch (black) - effective for high-value early crop but not economical for open field. 5) Crop residue from previous season can be left as surface mulch.

question: What safety precautions should be taken when applying herbicides to matter?
answer: 1) Wear PPE (gloves mask goggles). 2) Read label instructions. 3) Calibrate sprayer correctly. 4) Do not spray on windy days (drift damages nearby crops). 5) Avoid application before rain. 6) Clean equipment thoroughly after use. 7) Dispose containers properly. 8) Observe pre-harvest interval (PHI - usually 30-40 days). 9) Do not enter field for 24 hours after spraying. 10) Specifically: NEVER use 2

question: What are the major insect pests of matter in Pakistan?
answer: Major pests: 1) Pea aphid (Acyrthosiphon pisum) - most damaging. 2) Pea weevil/bruchid (Bruchus pisorum) - in stored seeds. 3) Thrips (Thrips tabaci). 4) Cutworm (Agrotis spp.) - seedling stage. 5) Armyworm (Spodoptera exigua). 6) Pod borer (Helicoverpa armigera) - occasional. 7) Leaf miner (Liriomyza spp.). 8) Red spider mite (Tetranychus spp.) - in dry hot conditions.

question: What is the economic threshold level (ETL) for major pests of matter in Pakistan?
answer: Pea aphid: 30-50 per plant or 20% plants infested. Thrips: 10-15 per plant. Cutworm: 2-3 cut seedlings per square meter. Pod borer: 5-10% pods infested. Armyworm: 3-4 larvae per square meter. Spray only when ETL reached (avoid unnecessary pesticides to protect pollinators and natural enemies).

question: How can I identify sucking pests (aphids whitefly thrips jassids) attacking matter?
answer: Aphids: Small (2-3mm) pear-shaped green/pink/black insects in colonies on young shoots leaves and flower buds. Sticky honeydew + sooty mold. Whitefly: Tiny white winged insects fly when plant disturbed. Yellow leaves. Thrips: Tiny (1mm) slender yellow/brown insects. Silvery streaks on leaves and pods. Jassids: Pale green wedge-shaped insects. Leaves curl downward with white edges (hopperburn).

question: What damage does the stem borer cause to matter and how to identify it?
answer: Stem borer (rare in peas). Damage: Larva bores into stem causing wilting of terminal shoot. Plant may break at bored point. Identification: Small hole near base frass (sawdust) around hole. Control: Remove and destroy affected plants. Not common in Pakistan peas.

question: What damage does the fruit borer / bollworm cause to matter and how to identify it?
answer: Pod borer (Helicoverpa armigera) - same as cotton bollworm. Damage: Larvae bore into pods eat developing peas. Identification: Holes in pods frass (black droppings) outside. Larvae green/brown with stripes. Pods shriveled with missing peas. More common in late crop (February-March). Control: Emamectin benzoate or Spinosad.

question: What damage does the leaf miner cause to matter and how to identify it?
answer: Leaf miner (Liriomyza spp.) - occasional. Damage: Larvae tunnel between leaf surfaces creating winding white mines. Identification: Blistered appearance white serpentine trails on leaves. Severely mined leaves turn yellow and drop. Control: Remove affected leaves. Cyromazine or Abamectin if severe.

question: What damage do armyworms / cutworms cause to matter seedlings in Pakistan?
answer: Cutworms: Larvae cut seedlings at ground level at night. Damage: Plants fall over as if cut by knife. Patchy missing plants. Armyworms: Defoliation - skeletonized leaves. Large larvae eat entire leaves. Identification: Larvae curled (C-shape) when disturbed in soil near damaged plants. Control: Chlorpyrifos drench around base.

question: What damage does the whitefly cause to matter and how to identify infestation?
answer: Whitefly damage: 1) Suck sap causing yellowing and stunting. 2) Honeydew leads to sooty mold (black coating on leaves) reducing photosynthesis. 3) Vector of viral diseases (rare in peas). Identification: Tiny white moths fly up when plant disturbed. Yellow sticky traps. Lower leaf yellowing. Sooty mold on upper leaves.

question: What damage does the red spider mite cause to matter and when does it appear?
answer: Red spider mite (Tetranychus spp.) - appears in dry hot conditions (Feb-March late season). Damage: Stippling (tiny yellow/white spots) on leaves. Severe: leaves turn bronze/brown and dry. Fine webbing on underside of leaves. Identification: Tiny red dots (mites) visible with hand lens. Shake leaf over white paper - moving specks. Control: Abamectin or Fenpyroximate. Avoid pyrethroids.

question: How do locusts and grasshoppers damage matter in Pakistan?
answer: Locusts (desert locust) and grasshoppers: 1) Defoliation - eat entire leaves and pods. 2) Can completely destroy crop in hours during swarms. 3) Grasshoppers cause irregular chewing damage. Identification: Presence of insects. Droppings on leaves. Control: Chlorpyrifos or Deltamethrin. District agriculture department issues alerts.

question: What are the signs of termite infestation in matter fields?
answer: Signs: 1) Dried dead plants that pull out easily with no roots. 2) Mud tubes on plant stems near base. 3) Hollowed stems. 4) White/cream insects inside roots/stem when dug up. 5) Patchy plant death. More common in rainfed areas and fields with crop residues. Control: Chlorpyrifos seed treatment or soil drench.

question: What are the signs of nematode infestation in matter roots in Pakistan?
answer: Root knot nematode (Meloidogyne spp.): Signs: 1) Galls (swellings) on roots (like beads). 2) Stunted yellow plants. 3) Wilting during day even with moisture. 4) Poor nodulation. More common in sandy soils. Control: Crop rotation (with marigold or cereals). Apply nematicides (Carbofuran) only if severe. Soil solarization.

question: How does the pest population in matter vary across different regions of Pakistan?
answer: Aphids: Severe in Pothwar (Punjab) and KPK - peak January-February. Thrips: More in Sindh and South Punjab (warmer). Cutworms: Problem in all rainfed areas. Mites: Late season (Feb-Mar) in Sindh and South Punjab. Pod borer: More in areas near cotton (Multan Bahawalpur). Whitefly: More in Sindh.

question: What pests are more severe for matter during the Kharif season?
answer: Summer matter (high altitude only): 1) Aphids (severe). 2) Mites (in dry periods). 3) Thrips. 4) Pod borer (Helicoverpa). 5) Armyworm. Cooler night temperatures reduce some pest pressure compared to plains.

question: What pests are more severe for matter during the Rabi season?
answer: Rabi (winter) pests: Aphids (most severe Nov-Feb). Thrips (Dec-Feb). Cutworms (Nov-Dec on seedlings). Whitefly (Nov-Jan in warmer areas). Pod borer (Feb-March late crop). Mites (Feb-Mar late season). Aphid population peaks in January-February when temperatures are moderate.

question: What pesticides are recommended for controlling aphids in matter in Pakistan?
answer: 1) Imidacloprid (Confidor) 250ml/acre. 2) Thiamethoxam (Actara) 80g/acre. 3) Acetamiprid 200g/acre. 4) Dimethoate (Rogor) 400ml/acre. 5) Malathion 500ml/acre (less toxic to pollinators - use when bees not active). 6) Natural: Neem oil (2-3 L/acre). Alternate products to avoid resistance. Spray when ETL reached (30-50 aphids/plant).

question: What pesticides are recommended for controlling whitefly in matter in Pakistan?
answer: 1) Imidacloprid 250ml/acre. 2) Pyriproxyfen (Planter) 200ml/acre (insect growth regulator). 3) Buprofezin (Applaud) 300g/acre. 4) Diafenthiuron (Polo) 300ml/acre. 5) Spirotetramat (Movento) 150ml/acre - systemic. Add mineral oil (300ml/acre) as adjuvant. Rotate modes of action. Use yellow sticky traps for monitoring.

question: What pesticides are recommended for controlling thrips in matter in Pakistan?
answer: 1) Spinosad (Tracer) 80ml/acre. 2) Fipronil 400ml/acre. 3) Imidacloprid 250ml/acre. 4) Thiamethoxam 80g/acre. 5) Acetamiprid 200g/acre. Spray when thrips damage visible (silvery streaks on pods). Early morning or evening application. Repeat after 7-10 days if needed.

question: What pesticides are recommended for controlling stem borer in matter in Pakistan?
answer: Stem borer is rare in peas. If present: 1) Chlorpyrifos 800ml/acre as spray. 2) Remove and destroy infested plants. Prevention: destroy crop residues after harvest. Not a major pest.

question: What pesticides are recommended for controlling fruit borer/pod borer in matter in Pakistan?
answer: 1) Emamectin benzoate 200ml/acre. 2) Spinosad 80ml/acre. 3) Chlorantraniliprole (Coragen) 60ml/acre. 4) Indoxacarb 150ml/acre. 5) Lambda-cyhalothrin (Karate) 250ml/acre. Spray at flowering and pod formation when eggs/larvae seen. Use pheromone traps for monitoring (Helicoverpa armigera).

question: What pesticides are recommended for controlling leaf miner in matter in Pakistan?
answer: 1) Cyromazine (Trigard) 150g/acre - specific for leaf miners. 2) Abamectin 200ml/acre. 3) Spinosad 80ml/acre. 4) Chlorpyrifos 800ml/acre. Spray when first mines appear. Best results when larvae are small. Remove severely infested leaves. Not usually economic in peas.

question: What pesticides are recommended for controlling red spider mite in matter in Pakistan?
answer: 1) Abamectin (Kingmit) 200ml/acre. 2) Fenpyroximate (Ortus) 250ml/acre. 3) Spiromesifen (Oberon) 300ml/acre. 4) Sulfur 80% WP 500g/acre (also controls powdery mildew). 5) Propargite (Omite) 500ml/acre. DO NOT use pyrethroids (they kill natural enemies and flare mites). Repeat after 7 days.

question: What pesticides are recommended for controlling cutworm/armyworm in matter seedlings?
answer: 1) Chlorpyrifos (Lorsban) 800ml/acre - soil drench around base. 2) Lambda-cyhalothrin 250ml/acre - evening spray. 3) Carbaryl (Sevin) 400g/acre. 4) Bait: Mix 1kg bran + 10g Carbaryl + 1L water - spread in evening. Apply when cutting damage first seen. Remove weeds around field (alternate hosts).

question: What is the recommended dose and spray schedule for pesticide application on matter?
answer: Aphids: Spray when 30-50/plant or 20% infested. Schedule: Dec-Jan peak. Pod borer: Spray at flowering (Jan-Feb) if >5% pods infested. Thrips: Monitor weekly spray at ETL. General schedule: Pre-flowering (Dec) for aphids. Flowering (Jan) for pod borer if needed. Use 100-120 L water/acre. Rotate pesticides every 15-20 days.

question: How should pesticides be mixed and applied correctly for matter pest control?
answer: 1) Fill spray tank 1/3 with clean water. 2) Add required pesticide dose (measure accurately). 3) Add adjuvant/wetter if recommended. 4) Fill to full volume while agitating. 5) Calibrate sprayer for 100-120 L/acre. 6) Use flat fan or hollow cone nozzles. 7) Spray in morning (6-9 AM) or evening (4-7 PM). 8) Avoid windy/rainy conditions. 9) Clean sprayer after use.

question: What is the pre-harvest interval (PHI) for pesticides used on matter in Pakistan?
answer: Common PHI: Imidacloprid: 14 days. Thiamethoxam: 14 days. Spinosad: 3 days (shortest). Emamectin: 14 days. Chlorpyrifos: 15 days. Lambda-cyhalothrin: 14 days. Abamectin: 14 days. For green peas: follow minimum PHI strictly. Do not harvest before PHI. For dried peas: longer intervals acceptable.

question: What are the bio-pesticides or organic alternatives for pest control in matter?
answer: 1) Neem oil (Azadirachtin) 1% - 2-3 L/acre for aphids whitefly. 2) Garlic-chili extract (10g garlic + 10g chili in 1L water boil strain dilute 1:10). 3) Tobacco extract (100g tobacco in 1L water soak 24h strain) - effective for aphids but toxic. 4) Entomopathogenic fungi: Beauveria bassiana (2g/L) for aphids. 5) Spinosad (bio-origin) for caterpillars. 6) Yellow sticky traps for whitefly/aphids. 7) Release ladybird beetles for aphid control.

question: How can pheromone traps be used for pest monitoring in matter fields?
answer: For cutworm: Use pheromone lures in delta traps (1 trap per 2 acres). For pod borer (Helicoverpa): Use sex pheromone lures (1 trap per 2 acres). Place traps at canopy height (30-50 cm). Check daily for moth catch. Spray when catch exceeds threshold (e.g. 8-10 moths/trap/night for borer). Replace lures every 4-6 weeks.

question: What safety equipment should a farmer wear while spraying pesticide on matter?
answer: 1) Chemical-resistant gloves (nitrile rubber). 2) Face shield or goggles. 3) Respirator (N95 or charcoal mask for organic vapors). 4) Long-sleeved shirt and full pants. 5) Apron or coverall. 6) Rubber boots (not cloth shoes). 7) Hat. Wash PPE after use. Never reuse empty pesticide containers. Shower after spraying.

question: What should a farmer do if accidental pesticide poisoning occurs during matter spraying?
answer: 1) Remove person from contaminated area immediately. 2) Remove contaminated clothing. 3) Wash skin with soap and water for 15 minutes. 4) If swallowed: Do not induce vomiting (unless label says) - give water. 5) If inhaled: Move to fresh air. 6) Take pesticide container to hospital (for identification). 7) Seek immediate medical attention. 8) Call Poison Control (115 or local emergency).

question: How should pesticide resistance be managed in matter pests in Pakistan?
answer: 1) Rotate pesticides with different modes of action (IRAC groups). 2) Do not use same pesticide group repeatedly. 3) Spray only when ETL reached (not calendar-based). 4) Use recommended doses (not sub-lethal). 5) Integrate biological and cultural controls (IPM). 6) Leave untreated refuges for susceptible pests. 7) Use pheromone traps for monitoring. 8) Avoid tank mixing unrelated pesticides.

question: When is the best time of day (morning/evening) to spray pesticide on matter?
answer: Best time: Early morning (6-9 AM) or late evening (4-7 PM). Reasons: 1) Bees and pollinators less active (protect beneficials). 2) Temperature moderate (15-25°C) - better efficacy. 3) Less evaporation. 4) Lower wind speeds. Avoid spraying: 1) Mid-day heat (>30°C). 2) Strong wind (>15 km/h). 3) When rain expected within 6 hours. 4) When leaves are wet (dew/rain).

question: What are the recommended fertilizers for matter cultivation in Pakistan?
answer: Recommended fertilizers: 1) Nitrogen: NOT recommended (peas fix their own N - excess N reduces nodulation). 2) Phosphorus: DAP (18-46-0) or SSP (18% P2O5 + 12% S) - critical for nodulation. 3) Potassium: SOP (50% K2O + 18% S) or MOP (60% K2O). 4) Sulfur: SSP or Gypsum (18% S). 5) Micronutrients: Boron (Borax) and Molybdenum (Mo) for nodulation. 6) Rhizobium inoculant (bio-fertilizer).

question: What is the recommended NPK dose per acre for matter in Pakistan?
answer: Recommended NPK: 15-20 kg N + 50-60 kg P2O5 + 30-40 kg K2O per acre. In kg/acre: N=15-20 P=50-60 K=30-40. Note: N is starter dose only (not full). For high fertility soils: N=10 P=50 K=30. For low fertility soils: N=20 P=60 K=40. Always adjust based on soil test.

question: What is the recommended dose of nitrogen (N) fertilizer for matter in Pakistan?
answer: 15-20 kg N per acre (starter dose only). This equals: Urea 35-45 kg (0.7-0.9 bag) per acre. Do NOT apply more than 20 kg N/acre. Excess N: 1) Reduces nodulation. 2) Lush vegetative growth (more disease). 3) Delayed flowering. 4) Lower pod yield. Apply all N at sowing (no top dressing). For soils with good Rhizobia: N can be zero.

question: What is the recommended dose of phosphorus (P) fertilizer for matter in Pakistan?
answer: 50-60 kg P2O5 per acre - most critical nutrient for peas. This equals: DAP 110-130 kg (2.2-2.6 bags) OR SSP 280-335 kg per acre. Apply full dose at sowing (basal). Phosphorus: 1) Promotes root development. 2) Enhances nodulation and N fixation. 3) Increases flowering and pod set. 4) Improves seed quality. On P-deficient soils increase to 70 kg.

question: What is the recommended dose of potassium (K) fertilizer for matter in Pakistan?
answer: 30-40 kg K2O per acre. This equals: MOP 50-65 kg (1.0-1.3 bags) OR SOP 60-80 kg per acre. Apply full dose at sowing. Potassium improves: 1) Water stress tolerance. 2) Disease resistance (powdery mildew). 3) Pod filling and sweetness. 4) Stem strength (lodging resistance). On sandy soils use 40-50 kg K2O.

question: When and how should the first dose of fertilizer (Basal Dose) be applied to matter?
answer: Basal dose applied at sowing time: 1) Full P and K + starter N (15-20 kg). 2) Apply in furrow 3-5 cm below and 2-3 cm to side of seed (drill placement). 3) If broadcasting: mix into top 5-10 cm soil during final cultivation. 4) Do not place fertilizer directly with seed (can damage germination and Rhizobia). Use DAP (contains N+P) for basal.

question: When and how should the second and subsequent doses (Top Dressing) be applied to matter?
answer: Top dressing is generally NOT required for peas due to N fixation. If plants show N deficiency (pale yellow leaves) at 20-25 days: apply urea 10-15 kg/acre as light top dressing. Do NOT apply after flowering. For P and K: all applied at sowing only. Excess late N reduces yield.

question: What is the role of zinc (Zn) fertilizer in matter cultivation in Pakistan?
answer: Zinc is essential for: 1) Auxin synthesis (IAA) for growth. 2) Pollen formation and pod set. 3) N fixation (Zn is cofactor for enzymes). Deficiency symptoms: small leaves interveinal chlorosis stunted growth poor pod set. Apply ZnSO4 5-8 kg/acre at sowing (mix with basal fertilizer). Foliar spray 0.3% ZnSO4 at 25-30 days for quick correction. Common in alkaline calcareous soils.

question: What is the role of boron (B) fertilizer in matter cultivation in Pakistan?
answer: Boron is critical for: 1) Pollen tube growth and fertilization. 2) Pod formation and seed set. 3) Sugar transport to pods. Deficiency: poor pod set hollow peas "brown heart" cracked stems. Apply borax (11% B) 2-3 kg/acre at sowing (mix with fertilizer). Do not exceed 4 kg - boron toxicity causes leaf burn. Foliar spray 0.1% boric acid at bud stage. Important in sandy and alkaline soils.

question: What micronutrient deficiencies are commonly observed in matter in Pakistani soils?
answer: Common deficiencies: 1) Zinc (Zn) - most common in calcareous soils of Punjab. 2) Boron (B) - in sandy and alkaline soils (causes hollow peas). 3) Iron (Fe) - in high pH soils (interveinal chlorosis in young leaves). 4) Manganese (Mn) - in organic matter deficient soils. 5) Molybdenum (Mo) - rare but affects nodulation (use Mo seed treatment). 6) Sulfur (S) - in intensively cropped low-OM soils (use SSP).

question: How can organic fertilizers (FYM compost Green Manure) be used for matter cultivation?
answer: 1) FYM/compost: Apply 10-15 tons/acre 15-20 days before sowing. Mix thoroughly into soil. 2) Green manuring: Sow guar (cluster bean) or dhaincha in July-August incorporate at 50% flowering (45-50 days) - adds 40-50 kg N/acre. 3) Vermicompost: 2-3 tons/acre at sowing. Organic sources improve soil health and reduce chemical fertilizer need. Especially beneficial for rainfed areas.

question: What is the recommended dose of farmyard manure (FYM) for matter in Pakistan?
answer: 10-15 tons (200-300 maunds) per acre. Apply well-rotted FYM (6-8 months old) 15-20 days before sowing. Spread uniformly and incorporate by cultivation. Fresh FYM should not be used (may contain weed seeds pathogens). FYM provides micronutrients improves soil structure water holding capacity and beneficial microbes - valuable for pea root health.

question: How does fertilizer application differ for irrigated vs. rainfed matter cultivation?
answer: Irrigated: Full P and K + starter N. No top dressing. Higher P (60 kg) for better root growth. Irrigated after fertilizer application. Rainfed (Barani): All fertilizer applied at sowing (no top dressing). Lower N (10-15 kg) to avoid vegetative growth. Band placement (not broadcast) for efficiency. Add extra FYM (15-20 tons) for moisture conservation. Use PSB (Phosphorus Solubilizing Bacteria) for P availability.

question: What are the signs of nitrogen deficiency in matter?
answer: Signs: 1) Uniform pale green to yellow leaves (starting from older leaves). 2) Stunted growth. 3) Poor nodulation (no pink nodules on roots). 4) Reduced branching. 5) Small pale pods. 6) Low protein content. Remedy: NOT N fertilizer (will reduce nodulation). Instead: ensure proper Rhizobium inoculation. If severe: light urea 10 kg/acre only once.

question: What are the signs of phosphorus deficiency in matter?
answer: Signs: 1) Dark green or purplish tint on leaves (especially underside). 2) Delayed maturity. 3) Poor root development. 4) Poor nodulation (few or no nodules). 5) Reduced flowering and pod set. 6) Small shriveled peas. Remedy: apply DAP or SSP at sowing in future crops. Cannot correct after sowing. Foliar spray 1% DAP solution (emergency).

question: What are the signs of potassium deficiency in matter?
answer: Signs: 1) Yellowing and browning of leaf margins (scorching) starting from older leaves. 2) Weak stems prone to lodging. 3) Small pods with shriveled peas. 4) Increased disease susceptibility (powdery mildew). 5) Leaf curling. Remedy: apply MOP or SOP at sowing. For severe: potassium sulphate foliar spray 0.5%.

question: What are the signs of zinc deficiency in matter?
answer: Signs: 1) Interveinal chlorosis (yellow between green veins) on young leaves. 2) Stunted growth with short internodes. 3) Small distorted leaves (rosette appearance). 4) Delayed flowering. 5) Poor pod set. Remedy: ZnSO4 5-8 kg/acre soil application or foliar spray 0.3% ZnSO4 at 25-30 days.

question: What happens if too much fertilizer (over-dose) is applied to matter?
answer: 1) Excess N: Excessive vegetative growth lodging delayed maturity poor nodulation reduced pod set more aphids lower yield. 2) Excess P: Induces Zn deficiency. 3) Excess K: Can cause Mg deficiency. 4) Excess fertilizer (any): Salt injury to roots leaf burn groundwater pollution wasted money. For peas: excess N is the most common problem. Always follow recommended doses.

question: What are the recommended fertilizer products (brand names) available in Pakistan for matter?
answer: 1) Urea: Sona Urea Engro Urea Fauji Urea (use sparingly for peas). 2) DAP: Engro DAP Fauji DAP ICI DAP (best for peas). 3) SSP: Pakarab SSP (good source of P and S). 4) SOP: Fauji SOP Engro SOP (for K and S). 5) MOP: Engro MOP FFC MOP. 6) ZnSO4: Fauji Zinc Engro Zinc. 7) Borax: Madak Borax. 8) Rhizobium: Nadeem Bio-Fertilizer, Ayub Rhizobium.

question: How should urea be applied to matter to avoid losses from volatilization (gas loss)?
answer: Urea is used only as starter N for peas (15-20 kg/acre). Application: 1) Apply at sowing (basal only - no top dressing). 2) Incorporate into soil by mixing during final cultivation. 3) Do not broadcast urea on surface. 4) Use neem-coated urea (slower release). 5) Apply DAP instead of urea + SSP (DAP contains N and P together). Better to avoid urea entirely if soil has good organic matter.

question: How many irrigations does matter require in total during its growing season in Pakistan?
answer: Matter requires 4-6 irrigations in irrigated areas. Rainfed (Barani): 0-2 supplemental irrigations if available. Irrigation schedule: 1st at 10-15 days (germination). 2nd at 25-30 days (vegetative growth). 3rd at 40-45 days (flowering - CRITICAL). 4th at 55-65 days (pod filling). 5th at 75-85 days (late pod fill - if needed). Stop after pod fill.

question: When should the first irrigation (Pehl-pani) be given to matter after sowing?
answer: First irrigation at 10-15 days after sowing (germination to seedling stage). Earlier irrigation (before 10 days) may cause seed rot and poor germination. Delay beyond 20 days reduces emergence and growth. In rainfed areas: rely on soil moisture - irrigate only if severe drought. Light irrigation (2-3 acre-inches) is sufficient.

question: What are the critical growth stages of matter that require mandatory irrigation?
answer: Three critical stages: 1) Flowering stage (40-50 days) - water stress causes flower drop poor pollination reduced pod set (30-50% loss). 2) Pod formation and filling (55-70 days) - stress reduces pea size sweetness and yield. 3) Germination to seedling (0-20 days) - stress causes poor stand. Avoid stress at these three stages.

question: How many days apart should irrigations be given to matter in summer (Kharif) in Pakistan?
