answer: Summer matter (high altitude areas only - Balochistan KPK hills): interval 7-10 days. Higher temperatures increase evapotranspiration. Light frequent irrigations (2-3 acre-inches) are better than heavy. Avoid overhead irrigation during flowering (9 AM-4 PM) to protect flowers.

question: How many days apart should irrigations be given to matter in winter (Rabi) in Pakistan?
answer: Winter irrigation interval: 15-25 days depending on soil type and temperature. Sandy soils: 10-15 days. Loamy soils: 15-20 days. Clay soils: 20-25 days. Cool temperatures (10-20°C) reduce evapotranspiration. Do not irrigate if soil is already wet (waterlogging risk) or if frost is forecast.

question: What is the total water requirement (acre-inches) of matter per crop season?
answer: Total water requirement: 400-500 acre-inches (10-12 million liters per acre). This is equivalent to 4-6 irrigations of 3-4 acre-inches each plus effective rainfall (100-150mm). Peas are moderately drought-tolerant but sensitive at flowering.

question: What irrigation method is suitable for matter in Pakistan — flood furrow drip or sprinkler?
answer: 1) Furrow irrigation: Best method - saves water prevents waterlogging and reduces foliar diseases. 2) Border strip/flood: Acceptable on level fields but can cause waterlogging on heavy soils. 3) Sprinkler: Excellent for sandy soils undulating land and frost protection - saves 25-30% water. 4) Drip: Best for high-value green pea production - saves 40-50% water and increases yield 15-20%. Avoid basin flooding on heavy soils.

question: How does drip irrigation improve the water use efficiency of matter in Pakistan?
answer: Drip irrigation saves 40-50% water compared to flood. Benefits for peas: 1) Precise water delivery to root zone. 2) Keeps foliage dry - reduces powdery mildew and other diseases. 3) Allows fertigation (water-soluble fertilizers). 4) Maintains uniform soil moisture - critical for pod filling. 5) Reduces weed growth. Setup cost: Rs. 120,000-150,000/acre with 60-80% government subsidy. High initial cost but profitable for commercial growers.

question: How should irrigation be managed during the flowering stage of matter?
answer: Flowering stage (40-50 days) is most critical. Management: 1) Ensure adequate soil moisture - avoid water stress. 2) Light irrigation (2-3 acre-inches) rather than heavy. 3) Avoid overhead sprinkler during peak flowering (9 AM-4 PM) - can wash off pollen. 4) Irrigate in morning hours. 5) Do not irrigate if strong winds or frost expected. 6) Water stress at flowering reduces yield 30-50%.

question: How should irrigation be managed during the grain-filling or fruiting stage of matter?
answer: Pod filling stage (55-75 days): 1) Maintain moderate soil moisture (not wet). 2) Stress at this stage reduces pea size sugar content and yield. 3) One irrigation at 55-60 days if no rainfall. 4) Avoid over-irrigation which delays maturity and increases disease (powdery mildew). 5) Stop irrigation 7-10 days before harvest for green peas (prevents pod splitting).

question: What are the signs of water stress (drought) in matter and what is the immediate remedy?
answer: Signs: 1) Wilting during day (leaves droop). 2) Leaves turn dull bluish-green. 3) Stunted growth. 4) Premature flowering and small pods. 5) Flowers drop. 6) Small shriveled peas. Immediate remedy: Apply light irrigation (2-3 acre-inches) immediately. If no irrigation available: spray water early morning (emergency). For severe stress: harvest early to salvage.

question: What are the signs of waterlogging in matter and how to drain excess water?
answer: Signs: 1) Yellowing of lower leaves. 2) Wilting despite wet soil. 3) Root rot (black/brown roots no white roots). 4) Plant death in patches. 5) Fungal growth on soil surface. 6) Poor nodulation. Drainage: 1) Immediately stop irrigation. 2) Open drains/furrows to remove standing water. 3) On flat fields: make temporary channels. 4) For future: plant on raised beds or ridges.

question: How should irrigation be managed after fertilizer application to matter?
answer: After basal fertilizer (at sowing): Irrigate within 5-7 days if no rain. Do NOT apply top dressing N for peas (only starter at sowing). If N deficiency occurs and urea applied: irrigate within 2-3 days. Apply irrigation when leaves are dry (morning). Light irrigation (2-3 inches) is sufficient - heavy irrigation leaches nutrients and causes waterlogging.

question: Should matter irrigation be stopped before harvest? How many days before?
answer: Yes stop irrigation 7-10 days before harvest for green peas. For dried peas (dal): stop 10-15 days before harvest. This allows: 1) Pods to mature uniformly. 2) Peas to develop sweetness (stress concentrates sugars). 3) Prevention of pod splitting. 4) Easier harvesting. Late irrigation delays maturity and can cause pod rot.

question: How does canal water vs. tube well (brackish/salty) water affect matter cultivation in Pakistan?
answer: Canal water: Best for peas - low EC (<1 dS/m) good for all growth stages. Fresh tube well water (EC <1.2): Acceptable. Brackish/saline tube well water (EC >1.5): Damages peas - causes leaf burn reduced germination and yield loss up to 60%. Peas are salt-sensitive. If only saline water available: 1) Mix with canal water (1:1). 2) Apply gypsum. 3) Better to avoid - choose salt-tolerant crops. 4) Use raised beds to reduce salt accumulation.

question: What is the average yield of matter per acre in Pakistan?
answer: Green peas average: 40-60 maunds per acre (1600-2400 kg). Progressive farmers: 70-90 maunds. Punjab (irrigated): 50-70 maunds. Sindh: 40-60 maunds. KPK: 35-50 maunds. Rainfed areas: 20-30 maunds. Dried peas: 15-25 maunds/acre. National average is below potential due to traditional practices and disease.

question: What is the maximum achievable yield (Potential Yield) of matter per acre under best management in Pakistan?
answer: Potential yield (green peas): 100-120 maunds per acre (4000-4800 kg) under optimal conditions (improved variety proper trellising irrigation pest/disease control). Research station yields: 100-110 maunds/acre. Progressive farmer yields: 80-90 maunds/acre. Yield gap between average (50 maunds) and potential (110 maunds) is 120% - large opportunity for improvement.

question: What are the main reasons for low matter yield in Pakistan?
answer: 1) Traditional low-yielding varieties (30-40 maunds). 2) Powdery mildew (30-50% loss). 3) Poor soil fertility (low P and OM). 4) No Rhizobium inoculation (poor N fixation). 5) Aphid infestation (20-30% loss). 6) Late sowing (after Nov 30). 7) Water stress (rainfed areas). 8) Dense planting (lodging and disease). 9) Improper harvesting (losses).

question: How can a farmer increase the yield of matter from 20 maunds to 40+ maunds per acre?
answer: Matter yield target is 40-80 maunds. To increase from 20 to 50+ maunds: 1) Use improved variety (Peas-2009 Meteor). 2) Rhizobium seed inoculation (fixes 60-80 kg N/acre). 3) Balanced fertilizer: 60 kg P2O5 + 30 kg K2O per acre. 4) Powdery mildew control (2-3 sulfur sprays). 5) Aphid control (at ETL). 6) Timely sowing (Nov 1-15). 7) Proper irrigation (4-5 irrigations). 8) Weed control. These steps can double or triple yield.

question: What high-yielding varieties of matter give the best production in Pakistan?
answer: Highest yielding varieties: 1) Peas-2009 (Ayub Research): 60-80 maunds/acre (green) powdery mildew tolerant. 2) Climax: 60-75 maunds medium maturity. 3) Meteor: 55-70 maunds early maturing. 4) Green King: 55-65 maunds export quality. 5) Rando: 50-60 maunds (late for hills). Avoid old low-yielding landraces (30-40 maunds).

question: How does timely sowing affect the final yield of matter in Pakistan?
answer: Each week delay after Nov 15 reduces yield by 5-10%. Nov 1-15 sowing: 60-80 maunds/acre. Nov 15-30: 45-60 maunds. Dec 1-15: 30-40 maunds. Dec 15+: 15-25 maunds. Timely sowing allows: optimum temperature during flowering (15-20°C) good pod set and higher sugar content. Early sowing (Oct) risks frost at flowering in north.

question: How does proper fertilizer management (Balanced use) increase the yield of matter?
answer: Balanced P and K (60-30 kg/acre) + Rhizobium increases yield by 50-80% over no fertilizer. Specific gains: P (60 kg) = +40% yield (root development nodulation). K (30 kg) = +20% yield (pod fill disease resistance). Rhizobium = +30% yield (N fixation). Zn + B = +10-15%. Combined effect: can increase from 30 to 70 maunds/acre.

question: How does proper irrigation management increase the yield of matter?
answer: One irrigation at flowering (40-45 days) increases yield 20-30% over rainfed. Two irrigations (flowering + pod fill) increase 40-60%. Three irrigations (veg + flowering + pod fill) increase 60-80%. In rainfed areas (0 irrigation): 15-25 maunds. With 3-4 irrigations: 50-70 maunds. Water is a major limiting factor.

question: What role does pest and disease control play in increasing matter yield?
answer: Powdery mildew (uncontrolled): 30-50% yield loss + poor quality peas. Aphids (uncontrolled): 20-30% yield loss + virus transmission. Combined pest/disease: can cause 70%+ loss (yield 15-20 maunds). Effective control: 2-3 fungicide sprays (sulfur) + aphicide at ETL = 40-60% yield protection. IPM practices save yield without excessive cost.

question: What are the best agronomic practices recommended by PARC/NARC for high-yield matter production?
answer: PARC/NARC recommendations: 1) Variety: Peas-2009 or Meteor. 2) Sowing: Nov 1-15 at 30 cm spacing 40-50 kg seed/acre. 3) Seed treatment: Rhizobium + Carbendazim + Imidacloprid. 4) Fertilizer: 60 kg P2O5 + 30 kg K2O + 15 kg N (starter) per acre. 5) Irrigation: 4-5 irrigations (germination vegetative flowering pod fill). 6) Powdery mildew control: Sulfur spray at first sign. 7) Harvest: at 70-80% pod fill.

question: How can improved seed quality (Certified Seed) increase the production of matter in Pakistan?
answer: Certified seed provides: 1) Higher genetic purity (>98%). 2) Higher germination (85%+ vs 60-70% farm-saved). 3) Disease-free (no seed-borne Ascochyta). 4) True-to-type (uniform maturity pod size). 5) Yield increase: 20-30% over farm-saved seed. Cost: Rs. 150-250/kg vs farm-saved Rs. 80-120/kg. Available at Punjab Seed Corporation and progressive dealers.

question: What role does soil health improvement play in boosting matter yield in Pakistan?
answer: Improved soil health (2-3% organic matter) boosts yield 30-50% through: 1) Better water holding capacity (critical in rainfed). 2) Higher nutrient availability (especially P S). 3) Improved soil structure (root growth and nodulation). 4) Beneficial microbes (disease suppression). 5) Reduced crusting (better emergence). Practices: FYM 10-15 tons/acre green manuring crop rotation minimum tillage.

question: How does the use of growth regulators (Plant Hormones) affect matter yield?
answer: Not commonly used in peas in Pakistan. Research shows: 1) Gibberellic acid (GA3) 20-40 ppm at branching - increases plant height (not needed). 2) Mepiquat chloride - reduces lodging in tall varieties but not commercial. Not recommended for general use. Focus on basic agronomy first.

question: What intercropping or relay cropping strategies can increase income from matter farming?
answer: 1) Matter + Wheat (2:2 or 2:4 rows) - reduces pest/disease by 25% and provides wheat income (10-15 maunds/acre). 2) Matter + Radish - radish harvested early (30-40 days). 3) Relay cropping: Sow matter into standing rice 15-20 days before rice harvest. 4) Matter as catch crop after early potato. Intercropping land equivalent ratio (LER) >1.5 - more productive than sole cropping.

question: What are the top 5 things a farmer can do to double the yield of matter in Pakistan?
answer: 1) Switch from traditional variety to Peas-2009 or Meteor (+50% yield). 2) Rhizobium seed inoculation (fixes N - equivalent to +30% yield). 3) Apply 60 kg P2O5 + 30 kg K2O per acre (balanced fertilizer) (+50% yield). 4) Control powdery mildew with 2-3 sulfur sprays (+50% yield protection). 5) Provide 3-4 irrigations (especially at flowering and pod fill) (+60% yield). Combined effect: 20-30 maunds to 70-90 maunds (2-3x increase).

question: How can precision agriculture or modern technology improve matter production in Pakistan?
answer: 1) Laser land leveling: uniform irrigation saves water 20-30%. 2) Soil testing: precise fertilizer recommendation saves cost. 3) Drone monitoring: detect powdery mildew hotspots early. 4) Variable rate technology: apply inputs based on soil variability. 5) Mobile apps: pest scouting records weather alerts market prices. 6) Drip irrigation (subsidized) - 40-50% water saving + higher yield. Adoption gradually increasing.

question: How does climate change affect matter yield in Pakistan and how can farmers adapt?
answer: Climate change impacts: 1) Warmer winters - reduced pod set. 2) Unpredictable rains - drought/flood. 3) Higher temperatures during pod filling - small tough peas. 4) Increased powdery mildew pressure. Adaptations: 1) Heat-tolerant varieties. 2) Shift sowing dates (earlier or later). 3) Supplemental irrigation. 4) Mulching for moisture conservation. 5) Climate-smart practices (zero-till intercropping).

question: What are the major fungal diseases (Uli) of matter in Pakistan?
answer: Major fungal diseases: 1) Powdery mildew (Erysiphe pisi) - most important and destructive. 2) Rust (Uromyces fabae). 3) Fusarium wilt (Fusarium oxysporum f.sp. pisi). 4) Root rot (Rhizoctonia solani Pythium spp.). 5) Ascochyta blight (Ascochyta pisi) - leaf stem and pod spots. 6) Downy mildew (Peronospora viciae). 7) Damping off (Rhizoctonia/Pythium) - seedlings.

question: What are the major bacterial diseases of matter in Pakistan?
answer: Bacterial diseases are rare in peas in Pakistan. Occasional: Bacterial blight (Pseudomonas syringae pv. pisi) - water-soaked spots on leaves and pods. Not economically significant. Fungal diseases are main concern.

question: What are the major viral diseases of matter in Pakistan?
answer: Viral diseases are rare in peas. Occasional: Pea enation mosaic virus (PEMV) - transmitted by aphids. Symptoms: mosaic pattern leaf distortion enations (vein swellings). Also Cucumber mosaic virus (CMV). Control by managing aphid vectors. Not economically significant in Pakistan.

question: How can I identify rust disease (Kungi) in matter fields?
answer: Rust (Uromyces fabae) - appears in cool humid weather (Jan-Feb). Symptoms: 1) Small brownish-orange pustules (uredinia) on lower leaves and stems. 2) Pustules turn black (telia) at crop maturity. 3) Yellowing around pustules. 4) Severe: premature defoliation reduced pod fill. More common in Pothwar region.

question: How can I identify powdery mildew in matter and what causes it?
answer: Powdery mildew (Erysiphe pisi) - most destructive pea disease. Causes: High humidity (60-80%) moderate temperatures (15-25°C) dense canopy. Symptoms: 1) White powdery coating on upper leaf surfaces (looks like flour dusted). 2) Spreads to stems and pods. 3) Leaves turn yellow then brown. 4) Pods become covered with white powder - peas small and bitter. 5) Premature defoliation. Appears from January onward.

question: How can I identify downy mildew in matter and what causes it?
answer: Downy mildew (Peronospora viciae) - less common. Symptoms: 1) Yellowish-green patches on upper leaf surface. 2) Purplish-grey fluffy growth on underside of leaves (sporangia). 3) Leaf curling and thickening. 4) Stunted plants. Favored by cool wet weather. Control similar to other mildews. Not a major problem in Pakistan.

question: How can I identify blight (early/late) in matter and what causes it?
answer: Ascochyta blight (Ascochyta pisi). Symptoms: 1) Small dark brown to black spots on leaves stems and pods (target-like concentric rings). 2) Spots enlarge coalesce causing leaf blighting. 3) Dark sunken lesions on pods (""pod spot""). 4) Seed infection (shriveled discolored). Favored by warm humid weather. Spread by seed and crop debris.

question: How can I identify damping off disease in matter seedlings?
answer: Damping off (Rhizoctonia solani Pythium spp.). Symptoms: 1) Pre-emergence: seeds rot before germination (patchy emergence). 2) Post-emergence: seedlings collapse at soil line (stem constricted dark lesion). 3) Infected patches in field. Favored by: wet cold soils poor drainage dense sowing. Control: seed treatment + avoid over-irrigation + well-drained soil.

question: What is wilt (Sokra) disease in matter and how to identify it?
answer: Fusarium wilt (Fusarium oxysporum f.sp. pisi). Symptoms: 1) Yellowing starting from lower leaves upward. 2) Wilting despite adequate moisture. 3) Brown discoloration of vascular tissue (cut stem cross-section shows brown ring). 4) Plants die from bottom upward. 5) Patchy distribution. Favored by: warm temperatures (25-30°C) low soil moisture. Soil-borne fungus persists for years. Use resistant varieties.

question: What is smut or bunt (Siyah-rooli) disease in matter and how to identify it?
answer: Smut is NOT a significant disease of peas in Pakistan. No economic impact. Focus on powdery mildew and wilt as major diseases.

question: What virus diseases affect matter in Pakistan and what are their symptoms?
answer: Occasional virus diseases: Pea enation mosaic virus (PEMV) and Cucumber mosaic virus (CMV). Symptoms: 1) Mosaic pattern (light and dark green patches). 2) Leaf distortion and puckering. 3) Enations (vein swellings) on leaves and stems. 4) Plant stunting. 5) Reduced pod set. Transmitted by aphids. No direct control - manage aphid vectors. Not economically important.

question: How do diseases spread from one matter plant or field to another?
answer: 1) Powdery mildew: Wind-dispersed conidia (spores). 2) Rust: Wind-borne spores (urediniospores) travel long distances. 3) Ascochyta blight: Seed-borne + rain splash + wind. 4) Fusarium wilt: Soil-borne (persists years) + infected plant debris + contaminated tools. 5) Damping off: Soil + contaminated seed + irrigation water. Prevention: clean seed crop rotation disease-free debris management.

question: What weather conditions (humidity/rain) favor disease development in matter?
answer: Powdery mildew: Moderate temps (15-25°C) high humidity (60-80%) but no free water on leaves. Rust: Cool (15-22°C) humid (>80% RH) with dew/fog. Ascochyta: Warm (20-28°C) wet conditions (rain/high humidity). Fusarium wilt: Warm (25-30°C) dry conditions (water stress). Damping off: Cool wet conditions. Jan-Feb foggy conditions in Punjab favor powdery mildew.

question: Which regions of Pakistan are most affected by matter diseases and why?
answer: Powdery mildew: Most severe in irrigated areas of Punjab (Faisalabad Lahore Gujranwala) and Pothwar due to dense canopy and fog. Rust: Pothwar region (Rawalpindi Attock) due to cool humid conditions. Wilt: More in rainfed areas and sandy soils. Ascochyta: Widespread but more in Sindh (warmer humid). Overall powdery mildew is the #1 disease across all regions.

question: What is the difference between nutrient deficiency symptoms and disease symptoms in matter?
answer: Nutrient deficiency: Symmetrical pattern often interveinal chlorosis uniform across field usually on older leaves first (N P K) or young leaves (Zn Fe). No pathogen signs (no spores mycelium). Corrected by fertilizer. Disease: Irregular patches pustules (rust) white powder (mildew) dark lesions (blight) often with pathogen structures. Spreads over time. Fungicides may help.

question: What fungicides are recommended for controlling rust in matter in Pakistan?
answer: 1) Tebuconazole (Folicur) 250ml/acre. 2) Propiconazole (Tilt) 250ml/acre. 3) Triadimefon (Bayleton) 200g/acre. 4) Pyraclostrobin + Epoxiconazole (Opera) 200ml/acre. 5) Mancozeb (Dithane M-45) 500g/acre - protectant. Apply at first rust appearance. Repeat after 10-14 days if needed.

question: What fungicides are recommended for controlling powdery mildew in matter?
answer: 1) Sulfur (80% WP) 500g/acre - effective cheap. 2) Tebuconazole 250ml/acre. 3) Propiconazole 250ml/acre. 4) Myclobutanil 200g/acre. 5) Hexaconazole 250ml/acre. 6) Dinocap (Karathane) 400ml/acre. 7) Azoxystrobin (Amistar) 200ml/acre. Apply at first sign of white powder (early January). Repeat every 10-14 days if needed. Sulfur is organic-friendly but avoid when temperature >30°C.

question: What fungicides are recommended for controlling blight in matter in Pakistan?
answer: 1) Mancozeb (Dithane M-45) 500g/acre - protectant. 2) Chlorothalonil (Bravo) 500ml/acre. 3) Copper oxychloride 400g/acre. 4) Propiconazole 250ml/acre. 5) Azoxystrobin (Amistar) 200ml/acre. Apply at early flowering stage. Repeat every 10-14 days if wet conditions persist. Use certified disease-free seed.

question: What fungicides are recommended for controlling wilt in matter in Pakistan?
answer: Wilt (Fusarium) is difficult to control with fungicides once symptoms appear. Prevention: 1) Seed treatment with Carbendazim 2g/kg + Thiram 2g/kg. 2) Soil drench with Carbendazim 500g/acre (early stages). 3) Trichoderma harzianum (bio-fungicide) 2kg/acre in furrow at sowing. 4) Use resistant varieties. 5) Crop rotation (4-5 years with cereals).

question: What bactericides are used for bacterial diseases of matter in Pakistan?
answer: Bacterial diseases are rare in peas. If bacterial blight occurs: 1) Copper oxychloride 400g/acre. 2) Streptomycin + Tetracycline (Agrimycin) 100g/acre. Not routinely needed. Prevention: clean seed good sanitation.

question: What is the spray schedule for disease management in matter in Pakistan?
answer: Powdery mildew: 1st spray at first sign (Jan). 2nd spray 10-14 days later. Rust: Spray when rust pustules seen (Jan-Feb). Ascochyta: Pre-flowering spray (Jan) if history. General schedule: Monitor weekly from December. Spray only when disease reaches threshold (e.g. white powder on 5-10% leaves). Use protectant fungicides (Sulfur Mancozeb) before disease arrives.

question: What is the correct dose and method of fungicide application on matter?
answer: 1) Calculate field area and required product dose. 2) Use 100-120 liters water per acre. 3) Add fungicide to water while agitating. 4) Use flat fan or hollow cone nozzles. 5) Spray to cover all leaves (upper and lower surfaces). 6) For powdery mildew: good coverage is critical. 7) Spray in morning (6-9 AM). 8) Avoid spraying during flowering if possible (protect bees).

question: What systemic vs. contact fungicides are recommended for matter?
answer: Systemic (absorbed by plant): Tebuconazole Propiconazole Azoxystrobin - curative (can be used after infection) longer protection (10-14 days). Contact (surface only): Sulfur Mancozeb Chlorothalonil Copper oxychloride - preventive (must be applied before infection) shorter protection (5-7 days). Strategy: Use protectants early then systemics when disease appears. Alternate both to prevent resistance.

question: How often should fungicide be sprayed during the matter growing season?
answer: Depends on disease pressure: Low pressure: 0-1 spray (only if disease appears). Moderate pressure: 2 sprays at 10-14 day interval (Jan-Feb). High pressure (powdery mildew): 3 sprays (Jan early Feb late Feb). Do not exceed 3 sprays to avoid resistance and cost. Stop spraying after pods are fully filled (70 days).

question: What are the bio-fungicides or organic disease control methods for matter?
answer: 1) Sulfur (organic approved) for powdery mildew. 2) Neem oil (0.5%) for mildew and rust suppression. 3) Baking soda (1%) + vegetable oil (0.5%) for powdery mildew. 4) Trichoderma harzianum (2kg/acre) soil application for wilt control. 5) Cow urine (10% solution) as foliar spray (traditional). 6) Milk spray (10% solution) for powdery mildew. 7) Crop rotation (3-4 years). 8) Resistant varieties.

question: When is matter ready for harvest in Pakistan?
answer: Green peas: 70-90 days after sowing (Feb-March in Punjab). Harvest when pods are well-filled bright green and peas are tender-sweet. Dried peas (dal): 100-120 days (March-April). Harvest when pods turn yellow-brown and peas rattle inside. Punjab harvest: Feb 15-March 30. Sindh: Feb-March. KPK: March-April. Balochistan: June-August.

question: What are the visual signs that matter has reached maturity and is ready to harvest?
answer: Green peas: 1) Pods plump and bright green. 2) Peas fill the pod (visible outline). 3) Peas are tender (press - not hard). 4) Sugar content high (sweet taste). 5) 70-80% pods at ideal stage. Dried peas: 1) Pods yellow-brown and dry. 2) Peas rattle inside when shaken. 3) Stems dry and brown. 4) Leaves dropped. Do not delay - over-mature peas become tough and starchy.

question: What is the recommended moisture content of matter at time of harvest?
answer: Green peas: Harvest at 70-75% moisture content (immature seeds). Dried peas: Harvest at 20-25% moisture (mature). For storage: dry to 10-12% moisture. For green peas: process within 6-12 hours of harvest to maintain sweetness (sugar converts to starch). Use moisture meter or traditional method (bite test).

question: How is matter harvested in Pakistan — manually (Daranti) or mechanically?
answer: Green peas (fresh market): Manual picking (labor intensive) - 20-30 laborers per acre pick pods over 2-3 pickings every 5-7 days. For processing (frozen/canned): Mechanical harvester (once-over harvest). Dried peas: Manual cutting with sickle (daranti) or combine harvester. Manual gives higher quality (selective picking). Mechanical reduces labor cost (Rs. 5

question: What machinery (Combine Harvester/Thresher) is used for harvesting matter in Pakistan?
answer: For green peas (processing): Pea combine harvester (specialized) - rare in Pakistan. For dried peas: 1) Combine harvester (e.g. New Holland) - settings: cylinder speed 400-500 RPM. 2) Reaper (tractor-mounted) + thresher. 3) Stationary thresher for manually harvested bundles. Most farmers use manual picking for green peas (higher value).

question: How should matter be harvested to minimize shattering or field losses?
answer: Green peas (manual): 1) Pick in morning (cool pods less brittle). 2) Hold stem while picking - don't pull vines. 3) Use both hands for speed. 4) Pick every 5-7 days (3-4 pickings). Dried peas: 1) Harvest at 90% pod browning. 2) Early morning harvest (dewy). 3) For combine: reduce cylinder speed. 4) Handle gently. Losses can be 15-20% if mismanaged.

question: What is the correct harvesting time for matter in Punjab?
answer: Punjab green peas: February 15 to March 30. Central Punjab (Lahore Faisalabad): Feb 20-March 15. South Punjab (Multan Bahawalpur): Feb 10-March 10. North Punjab (Rawalpindi): March 5-30. Dried peas: March 15-April 20.

question: What is the correct harvesting time for matter in Sindh?
answer: Sindh green peas: February 1 to March 15. Upper Sindh (Sukkur): Feb 15-March 15. Lower Sindh (Hyderabad Mirpurkhas): Feb 1-28. Warmer climate leads to earlier harvest. Dried peas: March 1-31.

question: What is the correct harvesting time for matter in KPK?
answer: KPK green peas: March 1 to April 30. Peshawar valley: March 15-April 15. Dera Ismail Khan: March 1-30. Higher elevations (Swat Abbottabad): May-June (spring crop). Dried peas: April-May.

question: What is the correct harvesting time for matter in Balochistan?
answer: Balochistan: Two seasons. Plains (Sibi Naseerabad) green peas: March 1-30. Highlands (Quetta Pishin) spring crop: June-July. Summer crop: August-September. Dried peas: harvest 10-15 days after green stage.

question: What post-harvest activities are done immediately after matter harvest?
answer: Green peas: 1) Pre-cool within 2 hours (reduce temperature to 4-5°C). 2) Sort (remove damaged pods). 3) Grade (size separation). 4) Pack in perforated plastic bags or crates. 5) Store at 2-4°C 95% RH. 6) Transport to market within 12-24 hours. Dried peas: 1) Sun dry for 3-5 days. 2) Thresh. 3) Winnow. 4) Clean. 5) Dry to 10-12% moisture. 6) Bag for storage.

question: How long after sowing is matter typically harvested in Pakistan?
answer: Green peas: 70-90 days after sowing depending on variety and climate. Early varieties (Meteor): 65-75 days. Medium (Peas-2009): 80-90 days. Late (Rando): 100-110 days. Dried peas: 100-120 days. In warm plains: shorter duration. In cool highlands: longer duration.

question: What are the common mistakes farmers make during matter harvesting in Pakistan?
answer: 1) Harvesting too early (small under-filled pods) - low yield and poor sweetness. 2) Harvesting too late (over-mature tough starchy peas) - poor market price. 3) Picking in hot afternoon - pods wilt sweetness lost. 4) Rough handling - pod damage bruising. 5) Leaving picked peas in sun - sugar converts to starch. 6) For dried peas: harvesting too early (high moisture mold in storage) or too late (shattering loss). 7) Not sorting - mixed quality.

question: How should matter be stored after harvest in Pakistan?
answer: Green peas (short term): 1) Pre-cool to 2-4°C within 2 hours. 2) Store in perforated plastic bags at 2-4°C 95% RH. 3) Shelf life: 7-10 days. For long-term: 1) Blanch (2-3 minutes in boiling water). 2) Quick freeze at -18°C. 3) Store frozen for 6-12 months. Dried peas: 1) Dry to 10-12% moisture. 2) Store in clean dry jute/hermetic bags. 3) Cool dry place. 4) Treat with neem leaves for insects.

question: What is the ideal moisture content of matter for safe long-term storage?
answer: Green peas: not stored long-term fresh (must be frozen). Dried peas: 10-12% moisture content for safe storage up to 12 months. Above 12%: risk of mold and insect damage. Below 8%: excessive seed cracking. Use moisture meter. Traditional test: bite pea - should be hard and crisp (not bendable).

question: What are the major post-harvest losses for matter in Pakistan and how to reduce them?
answer: Major losses: 1) Green peas: Sugar loss (10-20% in 24 hours at room temperature). Reduce: pre-cool transport in cold chain. 2) Mechanical damage (5-15%). Reduce: gentle handling padded crates. 3) Mold (10-20% in storage). Reduce: dry to <12% moisture. 4) Storage insects (10-15% over 6 months). Reduce: fumigation hermetic bags. Total losses can exceed 40% without proper management.

question: What storage structures or containers are recommended for matter in rural Pakistan?
answer: Green peas: Not stored fresh - sell immediately or freeze. Dried peas: 1) Metal bins (drum) - airtight rodent-proof best option. 2) Hermetic bags (PICS or GrainPro) - prevents insect entry. 3) Jute bags (gunny) - with inner polythene liner. 4) Clay bins (Godaym) - traditional. 5) Plastic silos (govt scheme). Avoid: direct floor storage damp rooms.

question: What pest control measures should be taken during matter storage?
answer: For dried peas: 1) Clean storage area before filling. 2) Dry peas to 10-12% moisture. 3) Mix neem leaves (1kg/100kg) or dried neem powder. 4) Use food-grade diatomaceous earth (1kg/ton). 5) Fumigation: Aluminum phosphide tablets (2-3 per ton) - only by trained person. 6) Pheromone traps for monitoring. 7) Inspect monthly for webbing live insects. 8) Never mix old with new grain.

question: What fumigants or storage pesticides are recommended for matter in Pakistan?
answer: For dried peas: 1) Aluminum phosphide (Phostoxin) - 2-3 tablets per ton. CAUTION: Highly toxic - use trained fumigator only. Seal storage for 5-7 days. Aerate 48 hours before use. 2) Malathion dust (2% active) - 250g per ton. 3) Deltamethrin dust. For small quantities: neem leaves camphor. Never consume treated peas.

question: How long can matter be stored without significant quality loss?
answer: Green peas (fresh): 7-10 days at 2-4°C. Frozen green peas: 6-12 months at -18°C. Dried peas: 12-18 months at 10-12% moisture in cool dry conditions. In hermetic bags: up to 24 months. In traditional jute bags: 6-12 months. In hot humid conditions: 3-6 months only.

question: How should matter be dried before storage to prevent mold and fungal growth?
answer: For dried peas: 1) Sun drying: Spread on clean tarpaulin or cemented floor in thin layer (5-10 cm). 2) Turn every 2-3 hours for uniform drying. 3) Dry for 3-5 days (depending on sun). 4) Test moisture: Bite test (crisp) or moisture meter (target 10-12%). 5) Do not dry on bare soil (contamination). 6) For large scale: mechanical dryers (hot air 40-45°C). 7) Cool peas before bagging.

question: What are the signs of spoilage or pest damage in stored matter?
answer: Signs of spoilage: 1) Musty or sour smell (mold). 2) Clumping or caking (excess moisture). 3) Discolored peas (dark brown black). 4) Sprouted peas. 5) Heating (warm to touch). Pest damage: 1) Holes in peas. 2) Fine dust/powder at bag bottom. 3) Webbing inside bag. 4) Live insects (weevils bruchids). 5) Empty pea hulls. Discard severely damaged peas.

question: What food safety practices should be followed during matter storage and handling?
answer: 1) Never use pesticide-treated peas for consumption. 2) Do not store in containers that held chemicals/fertilizers. 3) Keep storage area clean and rodent-free. 4) Do not consume moldy peas (may contain mycotoxins). 5) Wash hands after handling stored grain. 6) For frozen peas: maintain proper freezing temperature. 7) For fresh peas: maintain cold chain. 8) For dried peas: cook thoroughly before eating.

question: How does frost (Quora) affect matter and how can farmers protect it in Pakistan?
answer: Peas are moderately frost tolerant at vegetative stage (down to -3°C). Frost at flowering causes: 1) Flower drop (complete loss of that flush). 2) Damaged pods (empty or misshapen). 3) Stem cracking. Protection: 1) Sow at optimum time to avoid flowering during peak frost (Jan). 2) Irrigate before frost night (water releases heat). 3) Smoke: Burn moist crop residue upwind before dawn. 4) Use frost-tolerant varieties.

question: How does extreme heat (above 30°C) affect matter production in Pakistan?
answer: Peas are cool-season crop. Heat above 28°C: 1) Reduces germination (if at sowing). 2) Accelerates maturity (shorter duration). 3) Stops flowering and pod set (above 28°C). 4) Small tough starchy peas. 5) Increases powdery mildew. 6) Increases mite infestation. Avoid late sowing (Dec) that pushes pod filling into March heat. In Sindh/South Punjab: sow by Nov 15 maximum.

question: What are the drought-tolerant varieties of matter recommended for rainfed areas of Pakistan?
answer: 1) Meteor - early maturing escapes drought. 2) Local Desi (small seeded) - adapted to rainfed areas. 3) Peas-2009 - moderate drought tolerance. 4) R-17 (not matter - for linseed). For rainfed Pothwar: Meteor performs best. These varieties have deeper roots earlier maturity and osmotic adjustment. Yield under rainfed: 15-25 maunds/acre vs 30-40 for irrigated.

question: How should a farmer manage matter during unexpected heavy rainfall or flooding?
answer: 1) Immediately stop any irrigation. 2) Ensure drainage: Open channels to remove standing water. 3) If waterlogging <24 hours: plants may recover. 4) If >48 hours: root rot likely - assess survival. 5) After water recedes: apply light N (urea 10 kg/acre) for recovery (peas fix N but may need boost). 6) Monitor for fungal diseases (powdery mildew root rot) - prophylactic fungicide spray. 7) For flooded young crop: may need replanting if early season.

question: What is the effect of fog or cloud cover on matter growth in winter in Pakistan?
answer: Prolonged fog (Dec-Jan in Punjab): 1) Reduces photosynthesis (low light). 2) Increases humidity (promotes powdery mildew). 3) Delays maturity. 4) Can cause etiolation (stretched weak stems). 5) Reduced pod set. Management: 1) Wider row spacing (30-45 cm) for air circulation. 2) Preventive fungicide spray before fog period (sulfur). 3) Avoid dense canopy (no excess N). 4) Use disease-resistant varieties (Peas-2009).

question: How does hailstorm (Oola-bari) damage matter and what can be done after hail?
answer: Hail damage: 1) Bruised stems (entry point for disease). 2) Shredded leaves. 3) Damaged pods (split). 4) Lodging (flattened crop). After hail: 1) Do not harvest immediately - wait 5-7 days for recovery assessment. 2) Apply fungicide (Mancozeb) to prevent infection through wounds. 3) Light N spray (1% urea) for recovery. 4) If >70% damage: consider alternative crop (if early season). 5) Report to agriculture department for possible compensation.

question: What heat-tolerant varieties of matter are suitable for hot regions like Sindh and South Punjab?
answer: 1) Meteor - early maturing (65-70 days) escapes late heat. 2) Peas-2009 - moderate heat tolerance. 3) Climax - medium maturity but performs better in South Punjab if sown early. Key management: early sowing (Nov 1-10) to complete pod filling before February heat. Avoid late varieties (Rando). For Sindh: sow by Nov 15 maximum.

question: How should irrigation be adjusted for matter during drought conditions in Pakistan?
answer: During drought: 1) Prioritize critical stages (flowering and pod fill) - irrigate these even if skip others. 2) Apply light irrigations (2-3 acre-inches) rather than heavy. 3) Use furrow irrigation (not flood) - more efficient. 4) Irrigate at night - less evaporation. 5) Mulch with crop residue (3-4 tons/acre) to conserve moisture. 6) If only 1 irrigation possible: apply at flowering (maximum yield response).

question: What climate-smart practices are recommended for matter farmers in Pakistan?
answer: 1) Conservation agriculture: Zero-till/minimum till + residue retention (mulch). 2) Laser land leveling: Saves water improves uniformity. 3) Drought-tolerant varieties (Meteor). 4) Weather-based sowing decisions (use advisory services). 5) Micro-irrigation (drip/sprinkler) where feasible (60% subsidy). 6) Agroforestry: Trees on field boundaries reduce wind speed. 7) Crop diversification: Matter in rotation with climate-resilient crops.

question: What is the impact of late monsoon or early monsoon on matter cultivation in Pakistan?
answer: Matter is Rabi crop (sown Oct-Nov) so monsoon (Jul-Sep) does not directly affect growing crop. However: Late monsoon (rains extending into Oct) delays land preparation and sowing - causes late sowing yield loss. Early monsoon (starting Mar) can damage mature crop (Feb-Mar harvest) causing pod splitting and mold. Monitor forecasts and harvest promptly if early rains expected.

Contact provincial agriculture department.

question: Which research institutes in Pakistan have developed improved matter varieties?
answer: 1) Ayub Agricultural Research Institute (AARI) Faisalabad - developed Peas-2009. 2) National Agricultural Research Centre (NARC) Islamabad - developed Meteor. 3) Vegetable Research Institute Sahiwal - developed Green King. 4) Barani Agricultural Research Institute (BARI) Chakwal - for rainfed varieties. 5) Pakistan Agricultural Research Council (PARC) - coordination. 6) Sindh Agriculture University Tandojam - local varieties.

question: Where can farmers in Pakistan get certified matter seed?
answer: 1) Punjab Seed Corporation (PSC) - regional offices in Faisalabad Multan Lahore. 2) Provincial Agriculture Department extension centers. 3) Ayub Agricultural Research Institute Faisalabad (direct sale). 4) NARC Islamabad (for Meteor). 5) Vegetable Research Institute Sahiwal (Green King). 6) Progressive seed dealers (check certification tag). 7) Sindh Seed Corporation. Price: Rs. 150-250/kg. Demand certified seed early (Aug-Oct) as limited quantity.

question: What extension services are available for matter farmers in Pakistan?
answer: 1) Agriculture Department field staff (Agriculture Officers Field Assistants) - free advice. 2) Kisan Helpline 0800-15000 (Punjab) for queries. 3) SMS advisory services (CropMax Punjab) - weather pest alerts. 4) Farmer field schools (FFS) - hands-on training. 5) Agriculture extension WhatsApp groups. 6) Mobile apps: ""Agriculture Punjab"" ""Kisan Dost"". 7) Radio/TV programs (Zaraat Nama on PBC). 8) Demonstration plots at union council level.

question: What loans or credit facilities are available for matter cultivation in Pakistan?

question: What agricultural insurance is available for matter crops in Pakistan?

question: Where can a farmer in Pakistan report disease outbreaks or pest attacks on matter?
answer: 1) District Agriculture Office (Extension) - immediate reporting. 2) Plant Protection Department - for locusts/quarantine pests. 3) Kisan Helpline 0800-15000 (Punjab). 4) Agriculture Complaint Cell 0800-30000. 5) Local Agriculture Field Assistant (FA) - village level. 6) WhatsApp groups of agriculture department. 7) Crop Reporting Centre (for statistics). For powdery mildew outbreak: report early so advisory can be issued.

question: What role does the Provincial Agriculture Department play in supporting matter farmers?
answer: 1) Provide extension services (field visits training). 2) Distribute subsidized inputs (seed fertilizer). 3) Soil testing facilities (free/low cost). 4) Pest/disease forecasting and alerts. 5) Subsidy administration (Kisan Card drip irrigation). 6) Organize farmer field days and demonstrations. 7) Link farmers with credit and insurance. 8) Research linkage (recommend improved varieties). 9) Market information and price updates. Contact Provincial Director Agriculture (extension wing).

question: What is mustard and what is its agricultural importance in Pakistan?
answer: Mustard (Brassica juncea) known as Rai or Sarson is an important rabi oilseed crop in Pakistan. Its agricultural importance includes: 1) Edible oil (35-42%) for cooking. 2) Oilcake (high protein 30-35%) as livestock feed. 3) Green manure (quick biomass). 4) Condiment (mustard seeds for pickles and spices). 5) Low water requirement (2-3 irrigations) suitable for rainfed areas. 6) Industrial use (lubricants soaps). 7) Honey production (mustard flowers attract bees).

question: What are the main growing regions of mustard in Pakistan?
answer: Mustard is grown throughout Pakistan but major regions: Punjab: Sargodha Faisalabad Sahiwal Okara Multan Bahawalpur and rainfed Pothwar (Rawalpindi Attock Chakwal). Sindh: Sukkur Jacobabad Larkana Shikarpur. KPK: Peshawar Mardan Dera Ismail Khan. Balochistan: Nasirabad Jaffarabad Sibi (spring crop).

question: What are the climate and temperature requirements for successful cultivation of mustard in Pakistan?
answer: Mustard requires cool temperate climate. Optimum temperature: 15-25°C for vegetative growth 12-20°C for flowering and pod formation. Minimum for germination: 5-7°C. Maximum tolerance: 30°C (above this reduces oil content). Frost at flowering (>-2°C) damages flowers. Requires 300-400mm rainfall or irrigation. Dry weather at harvest essential.

question: In which season(s) is mustard cultivated in Pakistan (Rabi/Kharif)?
answer: Mustard is primarily a Rabi (winter) crop in plains of Pakistan sown October-November and harvested March-April. In high altitude areas (Balochistan KPK hills) it is grown as a spring/summer crop (Kharif) sown February-March and harvested June-July.

question: What is the typical crop duration/life cycle of mustard from sowing to harvest?
answer: Typical crop duration is 110-145 days depending on variety and climate. Early varieties: 100-110 days. Medium varieties: 115-125 days. Late varieties: 130-145 days. In warm plains: shorter duration. In cool highlands: longer duration.

question: What are the growth stages of mustard and what happens at each stage?
answer: 1) Germination (0-8 days): Seed absorbs water radicle emerges at 5-10°C. 2) Seedling (8-20 days): First true leaves root development. 3) Rosette/vegetative (20-50 days): Leaf expansion stem thickening. 4) Stem elongation (50-65 days): Rapid stem growth branching. 5) Bud formation (65-75 days): Flower buds visible. 6) Flowering (75-95 days): Yellow flowers open for 15-25 days. 7) Pod formation (90-110 days): Siliqua develop fill with seeds. 8) Maturity (110-145 days): Pods turn yellow-brown seeds harden.

question: How does mustard contribute to food security and the farming economy in Pakistan?
answer: Mustard contributes: 1) Provides edible oil (reduces import bill). 2) Oilcake improves livestock productivity. 3) Generates income for small and rainfed farmers (Rs. 60000-100000/acre profit). 4) Low input cost (2-3 irrigations) suits resource-poor farmers. 5) Green manure improves soil for subsequent crops. 6) Honey production (beekeeping). 7) Export potential (seeds and oil to Middle East).

question: How should land be prepared before sowing mustard in Pakistan?
answer: Land should be prepared to fine tilth. Sequence: 1) Deep ploughing with disc plough (if hardpan present). 2) 2-3 cultivations with cultivator. 3) Planking after each cultivation. 4) Laser leveling for uniform moisture. 5) Final planking just before sowing. For heavy soils: add 1-2 more cultivations and make raised beds.

question: How many ploughings are recommended for land preparation for mustard?
answer: 4-6 ploughings/tillage passes: 1 deep ploughing (every 2-3 years) + 2-3 cultivator passes + 1-2 plankings. In heavy clay soils: 5-6 passes. In sandy soils: 3-4 passes. Fine seedbed is important for small seeds.

question: What is the role of deep ploughing in mustard cultivation?
answer: Deep ploughing (25-30 cm) with disc plough: 1) Breaks hardpan and improves root penetration. 2) Enhances water infiltration and drainage. 3) Exposes soil pests (cutworms white grubs) to predators. 4) Incorporates crop residues. 5) Reduces weed seed bank. Do once every 2-3 years.

question: What is the recommended land leveling (Laser Leveling) method before planting mustard?
answer: Laser leveling is highly recommended. Benefits: 1) Uniform irrigation (prevents waterlogging in low spots). 2) Saves 20-30% irrigation water. 3) Improves germination uniformity. 4) Reduces weed patches. Field leveled to ±1 cm variation. Service cost: Rs. 2000-3000/acre. Subsidy available.

question: Should ridges and furrows be made for mustard cultivation in Pakistan? How?
answer: Ridges and furrows (raised beds) are recommended for heavy soils or high rainfall areas. Method: 1) Make 60-75 cm wide beds. 2) Sow 2-3 rows on each bed. 3) Row spacing 30-45 cm. 4) Furrow depth 15-20 cm. Benefits: prevents waterlogging improves drainage and reduces root rot. Not essential for sandy loam well-drained soils.

question: How should previously harvested crop residue be managed before planting mustard?
answer: 1) If previous crop was cereal (wheat rice maize): incorporate stubble by shallow ploughing. 2) Avoid planting mustard after other Brassicas (cabbage canola rapeseed) - minimum 3-4 year rotation. 3) Remove or deeply bury mustard residues after harvest (disease carryover - white rust Alternaria). 4) For rice stubble: manage with disc harrow + cultivator. 5) Do not burn residue - incorporate for organic matter.

question: What pre-sowing irrigation (Raunni) is required for mustard land preparation?
answer: Pre-sowing irrigation (raunni) given 15-20 days before sowing when soil moisture is low. Apply 3-4 acre-inches water. After irrigation: allow soil to reach field capacity then cultivate when moisture at good tilth. Saves 1-2 irrigations during crop growth. Essential for rainfed areas.

question: What implements and machinery are used for land preparation for mustard in Pakistan?
answer: 1) Disc plough (deep ploughing). 2) Cultivator (2-3 passes). 3) Disc harrow (clod breaking). 4) Rotavator (fine seedbed - use moderately). 5) Plank (leveling and moisture conservation). 6) Laser land leveler. 7) Ridger/bed planter (for raised beds).

question: How many days before sowing should land preparation begin for mustard?
answer: Start land preparation 15-20 days before sowing. Timeline: Day 1: deep ploughing (if needed). Day 2-5: first cultivation + planking. Day 7-10: second cultivation + planking. Day 12-14: pre-sowing irrigation (if needed). Day 15-18: final cultivation + planking + bed making. Day 18-20: sowing.

question: How does land preparation differ for irrigated vs. rainfed (Barani) mustard cultivation?
answer: Irrigated: finer seedbed required laser leveling important ridges for heavy soils pre-sowing irrigation optional. Rainfed (Barani): focus on moisture conservation - fewer cultivations (3-4 passes) deep ploughing for water storage no pre-sowing irrigation rougher seedbed to reduce evaporation mulching with crop residue. Use drought-tolerant varieties.

question: What is the recommended seed rate (kg/acre) for mustard in Pakistan?
answer: Recommended seed rate: 3-4 kg/acre for drill sowing. Broadcast: 4-5 kg/acre. Rainfed areas: 4-5 kg/acre (compensates for poor germination). For bold-seeded varieties: 4-5 kg/acre. For small-seeded (canola types): 2.5-3 kg/acre. Seed treatment essential.

question: What is the optimum row spacing and plant spacing for mustard in Pakistan?
answer: Row spacing: 30-45 cm (12-18 inches). For rainfed: 30 cm (closer rows). For irrigated: 45 cm (wider rows for branching). Plant to plant spacing: 10-15 cm after thinning. Target plant population: 150000-200000 plants per acre. Closer spacing for rainfed (higher plant density).

question: What is the recommended sowing depth for mustard seeds in Pakistan?
answer: Sowing depth: 2-3 cm (1-1.5 inches). In sandy soils: 3-4 cm. In heavy soils: 1.5-2 cm. Deeper than 5 cm reduces emergence. Shallower than 1.5 cm risks drying out or bird damage. Seed should be placed in moist soil.

question: What sowing method is best for mustard — broadcast (Chatha) drill dibbling or transplanting?
answer: Drill sowing is best: 1) Uniform depth and spacing. 2) Seed saving (20-25% less seed). 3) Better germination. 4) Easier weed control. 5) Higher yield (10-15% more). Broadcasting (chatha) is traditional but inefficient. Dibbling is labor intensive. Transplanting not practiced for mustard.

question: How should mustard be sown after a previous crop (e.g. rice-wheat or cotton-wheat system)?
answer: 1) After rice: Use zero-till drill to sow mustard into rice stubble. Allow 7-10 days for field to dry after rice harvest. 2) After cotton/wheat: Conventional tillage with 2-3 cultivations. 3) Ensure no herbicide carryover (pendimethalin from rice can damage mustard). 4) In rice-wheat system mustard can be relay cropped 10-15 days before wheat harvest. 5) Mustard after maize: excellent rotation.

question: Can mustard be sown using zero-till or minimum-till techniques in Pakistan?
answer: Yes zero-till is successful for mustard especially after rice. Benefits: 1) Saves 15-20 days and Rs. 3000-4000/acre land prep. 2) Moisture conservation. 3) Earlier sowing by 10-15 days. 4) Reduced weed pressure. Use zero-till drill with inverted T-type furrow opener. Seed rate: increase by 10-15% (3.5-4.5 kg/acre). Apply pre-emergence herbicide.

question: What equipment or tools (Seed Drill Planter) are used for sowing mustard in Pakistan?
answer: 1) Conventional seed drill (most common) - 9-11 row. 2) Zero-till drill (for after rice). 3) Bed planter (for ridge sowing). 4) Vegetable planter (precision). 5) Manual dibbler (small farms). 6) Pora (traditional). Calibrate drill for 3-4 kg/acre seed rate. Row spacing 30-45 cm.

question: What are all the major crop management activities for mustard from sowing to harvest?
answer: Timeline: 0-10 days: sowing seed treatment. 10-20 days: germination check gap filling first irrigation. 20-30 days: first weeding inter-cultivation. 30-40 days: top dressing N second weeding branching stage. 40-50 days: flowering - irrigation pest monitoring (aphids whitefly). 50-70 days: pod formation - second irrigation disease monitoring (white rust Alternaria). 70-90 days: pod filling - late irrigation if needed. 100-145 days: harvest.

question: What is the complete activity calendar (timeline) for mustard cultivation in Pakistan?
answer: October: land preparation (15-30 Oct). November: sowing (1-20 Nov). November-December: germination emergence gap filling (15 Nov-10 Dec) first irrigation (20-30 Nov). December: first weeding (1-15 Dec) inter-cultivation (15-31 Dec). January: top dressing N (1-15 Jan) second weeding (15-31 Jan) flowering (20-31 Jan). February: pod formation (1-20 Feb) second irrigation pest/disease monitoring. March: pod filling (1-15 Mar) late irrigation. March-April: harvest (15 Mar-15 Apr).

question: When should thinning (Gidai) be done in mustard cultivation and how?
answer: Thinning at 15-20 days after sowing when plants are 8-10 cm tall. Method: 1) Remove excess plants to achieve spacing 10-15 cm between plants. 2) Keep healthier vigorous plants. 3) Remove weak diseased and damaged seedlings. 4) Do not disturb roots of retained plants. 5) Irrigate lightly after thinning. Target population: 150000-200000 plants/acre.

question: When should earthing up (Mitti charhana) be done for mustard and why?
answer: Earthing up is generally not required for mustard. For tall varieties or high lodging risk: light earthing up at 30-35 days (after first irrigation). Method: pull soil around base of plants (5-8 cm high). Benefits: supports stems prevents lodging covers weeds improves drainage. Not practiced in rainfed areas.

question: How should inter-cultivation (Godi) be done in mustard fields?
answer: Inter-cultivation at 25-30 days and 40-45 days after sowing. Method: 1) Use hand hoe (khurpa) or wheel hoe. 2) Cultivate between rows at 5-8 cm depth. 3) Avoid damaging plant roots. 4) Also breaks soil crust removes weeds aerates soil. For large areas: use cultivator with adjustable tines set to avoid plants.

question: What is the process of transplanting mustard seedlings (if applicable) and when should it be done?
answer: Transplanting is NOT practiced for mustard in Pakistan. Mustard is always direct seeded due to taproot sensitivity and short growing season.

question: What is the optimal plant population per acre for mustard in Pakistan?
answer: Optimal plant population: 150000-200000 plants per acre (35-50 plants per square meter). For rainfed: 180000-220000 plants/acre (higher density). For irrigated: 120000-150000 plants/acre (more space for branching). Achieve by: seed rate 3-4 kg/acre + thinning. Higher population causes lodging and disease. Lower population reduces yield.

question: How is gap filling done in mustard cultivation if germination is poor?
answer: Gap filling at 10-15 days after sowing. Method: 1) Pre-soak seeds for 4-6 hours (for gap filling only). 2) Dibble 2-3 seeds per gap (missing plant area). 3) After emergence thin to 1-2 plants per gap. 4) Irrigate lightly after gap filling. 5) If gaps >30%: consider replanting (if early enough). Use same variety as original sowing.

question: When and how should staking or support be provided to mustard plants?
answer: Staking is generally not required for mustard as plants are 60-120 cm tall and self-supporting. For tall varieties (>150 cm) or high lodging risk: 1) Grow on raised beds. 2) Avoid excess N fertilizer. 3) Use lodging-resistant varieties (Raya Anmol). Staking individual plants is not practical for field crop.

question: What is pinching or pruning in mustard and when should it be done?
answer: Pinching (removal of apical meristem) is NOT recommended for mustard. It delays maturity reduces yield and is not practiced. Mustard naturally branches from base.

question: How should mustard be managed during flowering to maximize fruit/grain set?
answer: 1) Ensure adequate soil moisture (irrigate if dry). 2) Avoid pesticide sprays during peak flowering (9 AM-4 PM) to protect bees and natural pollinators. 3) Provide boron (foliar 0.1% boric acid) at bud stage if deficient. 4) Protect from frost (irrigation before frost night or smoke). 5) Manage aphids (honeydew interferes with pollination). 6) Avoid overhead irrigation which washes pollen.

question: What is the process of ratooning (Munda) for mustard in Pakistan? Is it recommended?
answer: Ratooning is NOT recommended for mustard. Unlike sugarcane mustard does not regrow after harvest. Secondary growth is poor low yielding and disease-prone. Always plant fresh seed each season.

question: How does crop canopy management improve yield of mustard?
answer: Canopy management: 1) Optimum plant population (150000-200000 plants/acre) prevents overcrowding. 2) Proper row spacing (30-45 cm) allows light penetration and air circulation. 3) Avoid excess N which causes dense canopy and disease (white rust Alternaria). 4) Inter-cultivation improves air circulation. Good canopy = balanced vegetative growth + high pod yield.

question: What field monitoring activities should a farmer do weekly during mustard season?
answer: Weekly monitoring: 1) Germination % (first 2 weeks). 2) Plant stand and gaps. 3) Weed presence and type. 4) Pest scouting: aphids (check young shoots and flower buds) whitefly flea beetles painted bugs. 5) Disease signs: white rust (white pustules on leaves) Alternaria blight (dark spots) powdery mildew. 6) Nutrient deficiency symptoms (especially S and N). 7) Soil moisture. Record observations.

question: What are the most commonly grown varieties of mustard in Pakistan?
answer: Commonly grown varieties include: 1) Raya Anmol (Punjab). 2) Punjab Sarson (PS). 3) Khanpur Raya (KPK). 4) Sindh Raya. 5) Dark Green Raya. 6) Local Desi (small seeded). 7) P-18 (high yield). Traditional varieties yield 8-12 maunds/acre.

question: What are the improved and recommended varieties of mustard approved by Pakistani agricultural research institutes?
answer: Improved varieties approved by PARC/NARC/Ayub Research: 1) Raya Anmol (Ayub Research Faisalabad) - high yield 15-20 maunds/acre oil 40% drought tolerant. 2) Punjab Sarson (PS) - 14-18 maunds/acre medium maturity. 3) Khanpur Raya (KPK) - suitable for rainfed. 4) P-18 (NARC) - high oil content 42%. 5) Sindh Raya (Tandojam) - salt tolerant. 6) Canola-type varieties: Rainbow Cyclone (low erucic acid).

question: What are the early-maturing medium-maturing and late-maturing varieties of mustard available in Pakistan?
answer: Early-maturing (100-110 days): P-18 Raya Anmol (early types). Medium-maturing (115-125 days): Punjab Sarson Khanpur Raya. Late-maturing (130-145 days): Sindh Raya Local Desi (hills). Early varieties suitable for double cropping (rice-mustard or cotton-mustard). Late varieties for high altitudes.

question: What high-yielding varieties of mustard give the best production in Pakistan?
answer: Highest yielding varieties: 1) Raya Anmol (Ayub Research): 15-20 maunds/acre white rust tolerant. 2) Punjab Sarson: 14-18 maunds/acre good for irrigated areas. 3) P-18 (NARC): 14-16 maunds/acre early maturing. 4) Khanpur Raya: 12-15 maunds/acre (KPK). 5) Sindh Raya: 12-14 maunds/acre salt tolerant. Avoid old low-yielding landraces (8-10 maunds).

question: What are the drought-tolerant varieties of mustard recommended for rainfed areas of Pakistan?
answer: 1) Raya Anmol - moderate drought tolerance. 2) P-18 - early maturing escapes drought. 3) Khanpur Raya - for KPK rainfed. 4) Local Desi - adapted to rainfed Pothwar. These varieties have deeper roots earlier maturity and osmotic adjustment. Yield under rainfed: 8-10 maunds/acre vs 5-6 for non-adapted.

question: What heat-tolerant varieties of mustard are suitable for hot regions like Sindh and South Punjab?
answer: 1) P-18 - early maturing (100-110 days) escapes late heat. 2) Raya Anmol - moderate heat tolerance. 3) Sindh Raya - developed for Sindh salt and heat tolerant. Key management: early sowing (Nov 1-10) to complete pod filling before February heat. Avoid late varieties. For Sindh: sow by Nov 15 maximum.

question: What type of soil is best suited for growing mustard in Pakistan?
answer: Well-drained loamy or sandy loam soil rich in organic matter is best. Deep fertile soils (45-60 cm depth) with pH 6.0-7.5. Mustard tolerates a range of soils but avoid heavy clays (poor drainage) and very sandy soils (low fertility). Good drainage is critical.

question: What is the ideal soil pH range for mustard cultivation in Pakistan?
answer: Ideal pH range is 6.0 to 7.5 (slightly acidic to neutral). Mustard can tolerate pH 5.5-8.0 but yields decline below 5.5 (aluminum toxicity) and above 8.0 (iron and manganese deficiency). At high pH >7.5: micronutrient availability reduced.

question: What soil texture (loamy sandy clayey) is most suitable for mustard?
answer: Sandy loam and loam are most suitable - provide good drainage aeration and root penetration. Sandy soils: require frequent irrigation and organic matter. Clayey soils: problematic due to poor drainage (root rot) and crusting (poor emergence). Silty loam is also good.

question: Can mustard be grown on saline or sodic soils (Kallar) in Pakistan? What are the precautions?
answer: Mustard has moderate salt tolerance (ECe up to 6-8 dS/m). On saline/sodic soils: 1) Apply gypsum at 50-100% GR based on soil test. 2) Use salt-tolerant varieties (Sindh Raya). 3) Pre-sowing leaching with 6-8 acre-inches good water. 4) Add FYM 10-12 tons/acre. 5) Use raised beds. 6) Avoid saline irrigation water (EC >2 dS/m). Not recommended on severely saline (ECe >10).

question: What soil drainage conditions are required for mustard?
answer: Good drainage is essential. Mustard is sensitive to waterlogging - 48-72 hours of standing water causes root suffocation and yellowing. Raised beds recommended in heavy soils or high rainfall areas. Good drainage prevents root rot and white rust.

question: How does soil organic matter content affect the yield of mustard?
answer: Higher organic matter (1.5-2.5%) improves: 1) Water holding capacity (critical in rainfed). 2) Nutrient availability (especially N and S). 3) Soil structure and root penetration. 4) Beneficial microbial activity. 5) Drought tolerance. Every 0.5% increase in OM can boost yield by 2-3 maunds/acre.

question: What soil testing should a farmer do before planting mustard in Pakistan?
answer: Essential soil tests: 1) pH and EC (salinity). 2) Organic matter. 3) Available N (NO3-N). 4) Available P (Olsen P). 5) Available K. 6) Sulfur (S) - critical for mustard oil content. 7) Zinc (Zn) and Boron (B) for deficient soils. Sample depth: 6-9 inches. Send to provincial soil testing lab (free or low cost).

question: How should soil fertility be maintained or improved for repeated cultivation of mustard?
answer: 1) Crop rotation: mustard after cereals (wheat maize) - not after other Brassicas (cabbage canola rapeseed) to avoid disease buildup. 2) Apply FYM/compost 8-10 tons/acre every 2-3 years. 3) Green manuring (guar dhaincha) before mustard. 4) Balanced NPK and S fertilization. 5) Incorporate crop residues (not mustard residues). 6) Use biofertilizers (PSB).

question: What are the signs of poor or unsuitable soil for mustard cultivation?
answer: Signs: 1) Water pooling after rain (poor drainage). 2) White salt crust (saline). 3) Stunted yellow plants (N or S deficiency). 4) Purple leaf margins (P deficiency). 5) Cracked clay surface. 6) Poor germination and seedling death (crusting or salinity).

question: What soil preparation practices improve the structure and health of soil for mustard?
answer: 1) Deep ploughing (25-30 cm) every 2-3 years. 2) Add organic matter (FYM 8-10 tons/acre). 3) Green manuring 6-8 weeks before sowing. 4) Gypsum application for sodic soils. 5) Laser leveling for uniform irrigation. 6) Avoid excessive tillage. 7) Raised bed preparation for heavy soils.

question: When is the best time to sow mustard in Punjab Pakistan?
answer: Optimum sowing: October 15 to November 15. North/Central Punjab (Sargodha Faisalabad Gujranwala): Oct 20-Nov 10. South Punjab (Multan Bahawalpur): Nov 1-20. Early sowing (Oct) risks high temperature poor germination. Late sowing (Dec) reduces yield due to heat during pod filling. Rainfed Pothwar: Oct 15-30.

question: When is the best time to sow mustard in Sindh Pakistan?
answer: Sindh: October 15 to November 30. Upper Sindh (Sukkur Jacobabad): Oct 25-Nov 15. Lower Sindh (Hyderabad Mirpurkhas): Nov 1-30. Warmer climate allows later sowing. Avoid December sowing as high temperatures reduce oil content. For spring crop: Jan-Feb.

question: When is the best time to sow mustard in KPK Pakistan?
answer: KPK: October 1 to November 15. Peshawar valley: Oct 15-Nov 15. Dera Ismail Khan: Nov 1-20. Higher elevations (Swat Abbottabad): March-April (spring crop) - sow after frost risk passes. Use cold-tolerant varieties.

question: When is the best time to sow mustard in Balochistan Pakistan?
answer: Balochistan: Two seasons. Plains (Sibi Naseerabad): Oct 15-Nov 30 (winter crop). Highlands (Quetta Pishin Kalat): March-April (spring crop) - sow after last frost (mid-March). Summer crop in high valleys: May-June.

question: When is the best time to sow mustard in South Punjab (Multan Bahawalpur DG Khan)?
answer: South Punjab: November 1 to November 20. Warmer winter allows later sowing. Sow by Nov 20 maximum. Delay to December reduces yield 1-2% per day due to heat stress. Heat-tolerant varieties recommended. For early market: sow Oct 25-Nov 5.

question: What happens if mustard is sown too early or too late in Pakistan?
answer: Too early (September-early October): 1) High temperatures (>30°C) reduce germination. 2) Vegetative growth excessive. 3) Early flowering in warm weather - poor pod set. 4) More pest pressure (aphids whitefly). Too late (December onward): 1) Shortened growing season. 2) Heat stress during pod filling - small shriveled seeds. 3) Lower oil content (35% vs 42%). 4) Lower yield (40-60% loss).

question: How does sowing time affect the yield and quality of mustard?
answer: Yield: Each week delay after Nov 15 reduces yield by 5-10%. Optimum Nov sowing gives 15-20 maunds/acre. December sowing gives 8-12 maunds. Quality: Late sowing reduces oil content (35% vs 42%) and increases erucic acid. Early sowing produces larger seeds but risk of frost damage at flowering in north.

question: What seed treatment (Zahar-alood) should be done before sowing mustard in Pakistan?
answer: Seed treatment is essential for mustard: 1) Fungicide for seed-borne diseases (Alternaria white rust). 2) Insecticide for early pests (aphids flea beetles). 3) Micronutrient coating (optional). Treat seeds 24-48 hours before sowing. Use 10-15 ml water per kg seed for uniform coating.

question: Which fungicide is recommended for seed treatment of mustard to prevent soil-borne diseases?
answer: Recommended fungicides: 1) Carbendazim (Bavistin) 2g per kg seed. 2) Thiram 2.5g per kg seed. 3) Captan 2g per kg. 4) Metalaxyl (Apron) 2g per kg - effective against downy mildew and white rust. 5) Tebuconazole (Raxil) 1.5ml per kg. These control seed-borne Alternaria and white rust.

question: Which insecticide is recommended for seed treatment of mustard to protect against early pests?
answer: 1) Imidacloprid (Confidor) 5ml per kg seed - controls early aphids and flea beetles up to 30 days. 2) Chlorpyrifos 2-3ml per kg - for termites. 3) Thiamethoxam (Cruiser) 4ml per kg - broad spectrum. 4) Carbofuran (Furadan) 3G 5g per kg - for soil pests (highly toxic - handle with care). For termite-prone areas use chlorpyrifos.

question: What is the process of seed treatment for mustard — dose method and timing?
answer: Process: 1) Calculate seed quantity (3-4 kg/acre). 2) Mix required fungicide + insecticide in 50-100ml water per kg seed. 3) Spread seeds on clean polythene sheet. 4) Pour solution gradually while mixing manually (wear gloves). 5) Ensure uniform coating. 6) Dry in shade for 1-2 hours (not direct sun). 7) Sow within 24-48 hours.

question: Should mustard seeds be soaked in water before sowing? For how long?
answer: Soaking is NOT recommended for mustard. Soaked seeds: 1) Swell and become sticky - clump during drilling. 2) Rot in cold wet soil. 3) Attract birds. Dry seed treatment followed by direct sowing is best.

question: How does seed treatment affect germination rate and early growth of mustard?
answer: Seed treatment increases germination from 60-70% (untreated) to 85-95% (treated). Fungicide protects from damping off and seed rot. Insecticide protects from flea beetles and aphids. Result: 15-20% higher yield potential and uniform stand.

question: What is bio-priming or microbial seed treatment for mustard in Pakistan?
answer: Bio-priming involves treating seeds with beneficial microbes: 1) Azotobacter or Azospirillum (N-fixers) - 1 packet (500g) for 10-15 kg seed. 2) PSB (Phosphorus Solubilizing Bacteria) - 1 packet for 10 kg seed. 3) Trichoderma harzianum (bio-fungicide) - 5g per kg seed. Mix with jaggery solution (50g jaggery in 1L water) as adhesive. Dry in shade. Reduces chemical fertilizer need by 15-25%.

question: How should treated mustard seed be stored before sowing?
answer: Treated seeds should be sown within 24-48 hours maximum. Do not store treated seeds for more than 7 days as fungicides degrade. If storage unavoidable: keep in cool dry place (10-15°C) in breathable (not plastic) bags. Never mix treated seeds with untreated seeds.

question: What are the safety precautions when doing seed treatment for mustard?
answer: 1) Wear gloves and mask. 2) Do not eat/drink during treatment. 3) Treat in well-ventilated area. 4) Wash hands thoroughly after treatment. 5) Keep treated seed away from children and livestock. 6) Dispose empty chemical containers properly (triple rinse then crush). 7) Do not use treated seed for oil extraction or consumption.

question: What are the major weeds (Khar-palwar) found in mustard fields in Pakistan?
answer: Major weeds: Broadleaf: 1) Bathu (Chenopodium album). 2) Maina (Asphodelus tenuifolius). 3) Peeli Buti (Fumaria parviflora). 4) Lehli (Sonchus asper). 5) Jangli palak (Rumex dentatus). 6) Kandiar (Convolvulus arvensis). Grasses: 1) Wild oat (Avena fatua) - most problematic. 2) Phalaris minor (Dumbi sitti). 3) Cyperus rotundus (Deela). 4) Cynodon dactylon (Khabbal grass).

question: What is the critical period of weed competition in mustard cultivation?
answer: Critical period: 15 to 50 days after sowing (from seedling to flowering). Weeds competing during this period cause 40-70% yield loss. First 30 days are most critical. Keep weed-free during this window. After 50 days mustard canopy closes and suppresses late weeds.

question: How does weed competition affect the yield of mustard in Pakistan?
answer: Weed competition can reduce yield by 40-70%. Heavy infestation: yield drop from 20 maunds to 6-8 maunds/acre. Grassy weeds (wild oat) are more damaging than broadleaf. Weeds compete for: water (critical in rainfed) nutrients (especially N and S) light and space. Also harbor pests (aphids) and diseases.

question: What are the recommended herbicides (Zahar) for weed control in mustard in Pakistan?
answer: 1) Pre-emergence: Pendimethalin (Stomp) 500-600ml/acre or Trifluralin (Treflan) 400-500ml/acre. 2) Pre-plant incorporated: Trifluralin. 3) Post-emergence (broadleaf): MCPA 300-400ml/acre (apply before flowering). 4) Post-emergence (grasses): Quizalofop (Topik) 300ml/acre or Fenoxaprop (Puma) 400ml/acre. DO NOT use 24-D on mustard - causes severe pod distortion and yield loss.

question: What pre-emergence herbicides are used for mustard weed control?
answer: Pre-emergence (apply within 3 days of sowing before weed emergence): 1) Pendimethalin (Stomp) 500-600 ml/acre - effective on grasses and small-seeded broadleaf weeds. 2) Trifluralin (Treflan) 400-500 ml/acre - incorporate into top 5-8 cm soil within 24 hours. Apply on moist soil. Do not use on sandy soils (leaching risk).

question: What post-emergence herbicides are used for mustard weed control?
answer: Post-emergence (apply at 20-30 days after sowing before flowering): For broadleaf weeds: MCPA 300-400 ml/acre at 3-5 leaf stage of weeds. For grassy weeds: Quizalofop ethyl (Topik) 300ml/acre or Fenoxaprop (Puma) 400ml/acre. DO NOT use 24-D (causes severe pod distortion). Do not spray after bud formation (45 days).

question: What is the correct dose and timing of herbicide application in mustard?
answer: Pendimethalin: 500-600 ml/acre within 3 days of sowing. MCPA: 300-400 ml/acre at 20-30 days (weed 3-5 leaf). Quizalofop: 300ml/acre at 20-30 days for grass weeds. Use 100-120 liters water/acre. Flat fan nozzle. Apply in morning when no wind/rain. Do not spray after flowering.

question: How should manual weeding (Khurpa/Godi) be done in mustard fields?
answer: Manual weeding: 1st weeding at 20-25 days (after thinning). 2nd weeding at 40-45 days (before flowering). Method: 1) Use khurpa (hand hoe) to cut weeds just below soil surface. 2) Remove weeds from field (don't leave uprooted weeds). 3) Be careful not to disturb mustard roots. 4) Weeding also aerates soil. Labor requirement: 15-20 person-days/acre for two weedings.

question: How many manual weedings are recommended for mustard cultivation in Pakistan?
answer: Two manual weedings are recommended: 1st at 20-25 days after sowing. 2nd at 40-45 days after sowing. In low weed pressure areas: one weeding at 25-30 days may suffice. In heavy weed infestation: two weedings + pre-emergence herbicide. Rainfed areas: timely weeding critical due to limited moisture.

question: What mechanical methods (Weeders) can be used for weed control in mustard?
answer: 1) Wheel hoe (hand-operated) - for row spacing 30-45 cm. 2) Tractor-drawn cultivator with adjustable tines - for large fields (set to avoid plant rows). 3) Cono-weeder (for narrow rows). Mechanical weeding at 25-30 and 40-45 days. Inter-cultivation should be shallow (5-8 cm) to avoid root damage. Followed by manual removal of intra-row weeds.

question: How can mulching help control weeds in mustard cultivation?
answer: Mulching is effective for mustard: 1) Straw mulch (wheat/rice) at 3-4 tons/acre applied after sowing suppresses weeds. 2) Reduces weed germination by blocking light. 3) Also conserves soil moisture (valuable for rainfed). 4) Plastic mulch not economical for mustard. 5) Crop residue from previous season can be left as surface mulch.

question: What safety precautions should be taken when applying herbicides to mustard?
answer: 1) Wear PPE (gloves mask goggles). 2) Read label instructions. 3) Calibrate sprayer correctly. 4) Do not spray on windy days (drift damages nearby crops). 5) Avoid application before rain. 6) Clean equipment thoroughly after use. 7) Dispose containers properly. 8) Observe pre-harvest interval (PHI - usually 30-40 days). 9) Do not enter field for 24 hours after spraying. 10) Specifically: NEVER use 24-D on mustard.

question: What are the major insect pests of mustard in Pakistan?
answer: Major pests: 1) Mustard aphid (Lipaphis erysimi) - most damaging. 2) Painted bug (Bagrada hilaris). 3) Flea beetle (Phyllotreta spp.) - seedling stage. 4) Whitefly (Bemisia tabaci). 5) Cutworm (Agrotis spp.) - seedling stage. 6) Pod borer (Helicoverpa armigera) - occasional. 7) Leaf miner (Liriomyza spp.). 8) Red spider mite (Tetranychus spp.) - in dry conditions.

question: What is the economic threshold level (ETL) for major pests of mustard in Pakistan?
answer: Mustard aphid: 30-50 per plant or 20% plants infested. Painted bug: 5-10 per plant. Flea beetle: 5-10% leaf area damaged. Whitefly: 5-10 per leaf. Cutworm: 2-3 cut seedlings per square meter. Pod borer: 5-10% pods infested. Spray only when ETL reached (avoid unnecessary pesticides to protect pollinators).

question: How can I identify sucking pests (aphids whitefly thrips jassids) attacking mustard?
answer: Aphids: Small (2-3mm) pear-shaped green/black insects in colonies on young leaves stems and flower buds. Sticky honeydew + sooty mold. Whitefly: Tiny white winged insects fly when plant disturbed. Yellow leaves. Thrips: Tiny (1mm) slender yellow/brown insects. Silvery streaks on leaves and pods. Jassids: Pale green wedge-shaped insects. Leaves curl downward with white edges.

question: What damage does the stem borer cause to mustard and how to identify it?
answer: Stem borer (rare in mustard). Damage: Larva bores into stem causing wilting of terminal shoot. Plant may break at bored point. Identification: Small hole near base frass (sawdust) around hole. Control: Remove and destroy affected plants. Not common in Pakistan mustard.

question: What damage does the fruit borer / bollworm cause to mustard and how to identify it?
answer: Pod borer (Helicoverpa armigera) - same as cotton bollworm. Damage: Larvae bore into pods eat developing seeds. Identification: Holes in pods frass (black droppings) outside. Larvae green/brown with stripes. Pods shriveled with missing seeds. More common in late crop (February-March). Control: Emamectin benzoate or Spinosad.

question: What damage does the leaf miner cause to mustard and how to identify it?
answer: Leaf miner (Liriomyza spp.) - occasional. Damage: Larvae tunnel between leaf surfaces creating winding white mines. Identification: Blistered appearance white serpentine trails on leaves. Severely mined leaves turn yellow and drop. Control: Remove affected leaves. Cyromazine or Abamectin if severe.

question: What damage do armyworms / cutworms cause to mustard seedlings in Pakistan?
answer: Cutworms: Larvae cut seedlings at ground level at night. Damage: Plants fall over as if cut by knife. Patchy missing plants. Armyworms: Defoliation - skeletonized leaves. Identification: Larvae curled (C-shape) when disturbed in soil near damaged plants. Control: Chlorpyrifos drench around base.

question: What damage does the whitefly cause to mustard and how to identify infestation?
answer: Whitefly damage: 1) Suck sap causing yellowing and stunting. 2) Honeydew leads to sooty mold (black coating on leaves) reducing photosynthesis. 3) Vector of viral diseases (rare in mustard). Identification: Tiny white moths fly up when plant disturbed. Yellow sticky traps. Lower leaf yellowing. Sooty mold on upper leaves.

question: What damage does the red spider mite cause to mustard and when does it appear?
answer: Red spider mite (Tetranychus spp.) - appears in dry hot conditions (Feb-March late season). Damage: Stippling (tiny yellow/white spots) on leaves. Severe: leaves turn bronze/brown and dry. Fine webbing on underside. Identification: Tiny red dots visible with hand lens. Shake leaf over white paper - moving specks. Control: Abamectin or Fenpyroximate. Avoid pyrethroids.

question: How do locusts and grasshoppers damage mustard in Pakistan?
answer: Locusts (desert locust) and grasshoppers: 1) Defoliation - eat entire leaves and pods. 2) Can completely destroy crop in hours during swarms. 3) Grasshoppers cause irregular chewing damage. Identification: Presence of insects. Droppings on leaves. Control: Chlorpyrifos or Deltamethrin. District agriculture department issues alerts.

question: What are the signs of termite infestation in mustard fields?
answer: Signs: 1) Dried dead plants that pull out easily with no roots. 2) Mud tubes on plant stems near base. 3) Hollowed stems. 4) White/cream insects inside roots/stem when dug up. 5) Patchy plant death. More common in rainfed areas and fields with crop residues. Control: Chlorpyrifos seed treatment or soil drench.

question: What are the signs of nematode infestation in mustard roots in Pakistan?
answer: Root knot nematode (Meloidogyne spp.): Signs: 1) Galls (swellings) on roots (like beads). 2) Stunted yellow plants. 3) Wilting during day even with moisture. More common in sandy soils. Control: Crop rotation (with marigold or cereals). Apply nematicides (Carbofuran) only if severe. Soil solarization.

question: How does the pest population in mustard vary across different regions of Pakistan?
answer: Aphids: Severe in Pothwar (Punjab) and KPK - peak January-February. Painted bug: More in Sindh and South Punjab. Flea beetle: Problem in all rainfed areas at seedling stage.
